Return to school/nursery: 48 hours after LAST episode of diarrhoea or vomiting
NEVER GIVE: loperamide to children under 2 years; aspirin; high-dose glucose drinks; plain water alone to severely dehydrated infants (worsens hyponatraemia)

Elderly patients are at high risk of severe dehydration from reduced thirst sensation; impaired renal concentrating ability; multiple comorbidities; polypharmacy (PPIs, diuretics — worsen dehydration risk)
C. DIFFICILE is predominantly a disease of the elderly on antibiotics — any antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in a patient over 65 should be tested for C. diff

Dehydration signs may be less obvious in the elderly — reduced skin turgor is normal in aged skin (less reliable sign); check blood pressure lying and standing (postural drop = dehydration); serum creatinine rising

NOROVIRUS in elderly care homes is extremely dangerous — outbreaks cause significant mortality; strict infection control (48-hour exclusion; bleach cleaning; isolation of symptomatic residents); cohorting in healthcare settings
Confusion and delirium from dehydration and electrolyte disturbances are common presenting features in elderly gastroenteritis — not just GI symptoms
Lower threshold for hospital admission; faster deterioration; multiple comorbidities

Listeria monocytogenes — most concerning bacterial pathogen in pregnancy; causes severe invasive gastroenteritis; miscarriage; premature birth; stillbirth; neonatal meningitis; any febrile illness after eating high-risk foods (soft cheese, deli meats, smoked fish) in pregnancy warrants URGENT assessment and empirical IV ampicillin
Salmonella and Campylobacter may cause bacteraemia in pregnancy — treat with azithromycin (safe in all trimesters); avoid fluoroquinolones
Dehydration in pregnancy triggers uterine contractions — severe gastroenteritis dehydration may precipitate preterm labour; aggressive IV fluid replacement essential

SAFE ANTIBIOTICS in pregnancy for gastroenteritis: amoxicillin; azithromycin; cefalexin; cephalosporins; ampicillin (Listeria); AVOID: fluoroquinolones (1st trimester — teratogenicity concerns); tetracycline; nitrofurantoin at term
ORS is safe in all trimesters; IV Ringer's Lactate for severe dehydration; paracetamol for fever
Norovirus and viral gastroenteritis — supportive management; monitor foetal heart rate in severe illness
Giardia in pregnancy: tinidazole preferred over metronidazole (metronidazole — avoid in 1st trimester if possible)

HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200): Cryptosporidium causes severe, chronic, life-threatening diarrhoea without effective specific antibiotic treatment; only effective treatment is immune reconstitution via ART; CMV colitis (bloody diarrhoea — diagnose by colonoscopy biopsy; treat with IV ganciclovir); atypical Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) — diarrhoea + fever + weight loss in AIDS; Microsporidia; Cyclospora
Organ transplant recipients: C. difficile is extremely common; CMV gastroenteritis; Cryptosporidium; lower threshold for investigations and treatment; risk of unusual organisms

Chemotherapy patients: C. difficile from prophylactic antibiotics and chemotherapy-related gut flora disruption; consider gut decontamination protocol changes; neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) — must be distinguished from infectious gastroenteritis
ALL immunocompromised patients with gastroenteritis require: hospitalisation; blood cultures; comprehensive stool PCR panel; endoscopy if not improving; early specialist involvement

when_to_see_doctor: Any blood or mucus in stools — DO NOT manage at home without medical assessment; possible Shigella, Campylobacter, STEC, amoebic dysentery — some require specific antibiotics; others (STEC) should NOT receive antibiotics
Infant under 3 months with diarrhoea or vomiting — ALWAYS see a doctor SAME DAY; very limited fluid reserves; high risk of rapid deterioration
Child not able to keep any ORS down for more than 1-2 hours — vomiting everything; needs antiemetic (ondansetron) and/or IV fluids
Signs of moderate dehydration developing — sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine output, increasingly lethargic — GP or urgent care same day
High fever >38.5°C with gastroenteritis — possible invasive bacterial infection requiring specific treatment
Diarrhoea lasting more than 3 days in children or 5-7 days in adults without improvement
Prolonged diarrhoea >14 days — possible parasitic infection (Giardia, Entamoeba, Cryptosporidium) — stool examination required
Recent use of antibiotics within 2 months AND new diarrhoea — possible C. difficile; stool toxin testing required
Immunocompromised patient (HIV, cancer, transplant) with any gastroenteritis — higher risk of severe and unusual infections
Recently returned from travel abroad with persistent diarrhoea >7 days — possible tropical infection (Giardia, Entamoeba, typhoid, Cyclospora)
Food handler or healthcare worker with gastroenteritis — occupational health requirements; potential source of outbreak; needs stool culture results before returning to work
Multiple people in the same household or institution ill simultaneously after eating the same food — suspected food poisoning outbreak; contact local health department or FSSAI food safety officer
emergency_signs: NO URINE OUTPUT for 8+ hours in a child, OR visibly very dark concentrated urine with sunken eyes and unable to drink — SEVERE DEHYDRATION — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112) IMMEDIATELY
INFANT UNCONSCIOUS, LIMP, OR UNABLE TO ROUSE — severe dehydration shock or electrolyte crisis — CALL 102/112
BLOOD IN STOOL IN A CHILD who was getting better but now becoming PALE, BRUISING, AND STOPPING URINATING 5-7 days after the onset — POSSIBLE HUS (Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome) — PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCY
CONFUSION or ALTERED CONSCIOUSNESS in an adult or older child with gastroenteritis — dehydration shock; hyponatraemia; bacteraemia — EMERGENCY
RAPID WEAK PULSE, HYPOTENSION (feeling faint), COLD CLAMMY EXTREMITIES with gastroenteritis — DEHYDRATION SHOCK — CALL 102/112
MASSIVE PROFUSE WATERY DIARRHOEA — litres per hour — possible CHOLERA — EMERGENCY IV fluids; call 102/112
ASCENDING WEAKNESS or PARALYSIS in the legs, weeks after a diarrhoeal illness — possible GUILLAIN-BARRÉ SYNDROME post-Campylobacter — URGENT NEUROLOGY REFERRAL
SEVERE GENERALISED ABDOMINAL PAIN WITH RIGID ABDOMEN ('board-like') and absent bowel sounds in a patient with known C. difficile — POSSIBLE TOXIC MEGACOLON or PERFORATION — SURGICAL EMERGENCY
HIGH FEVER (>39°C) WITH RIGORS (violent shivering) AND BLOODY DIARRHOEA — POSSIBLE BACTERAEMIA — blood cultures and IV antibiotics needed URGENTLY
PREGNANT WOMAN with fever + gastroenteritis after eating soft cheese, deli meats, or smoked fish — POSSIBLE LISTERIA — OBSTETRIC AND INFECTIOUS DISEASE EMERGENCY

faq.question: What is the difference between gastroenteritis and food poisoning?
faq.answer: Gastroenteritis is a broader term — inflammation of the stomach and intestines causing diarrhoea and vomiting from any cause, including viruses, bacteria, parasites, or their toxins. Food poisoning is specifically when illness is caused by eating contaminated food or drink. In practice there is significant overlap — most food poisoning IS a form of gastroenteritis. The key clinical distinction is timing: food poisoning from PRE-FORMED TOXINS (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) starts very quickly — within 1-6 hours of eating, with explosive vomiting as the dominant symptom. Gastroenteritis from viral infections (norovirus, rotavirus) or bacterial invasion has a longer incubation of 12 hours to several days. A useful rule: if multiple people who ate the same meal all become ill within 6 hours — think food poisoning from toxins; if illness develops 24-72 hours after eating and spreads through a household — think viral gastroenteritis or bacterial infection.

faq.question: What is ORS and why is it more important than any medicine?
faq.answer: ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) is a simple mixture of glucose, sodium, potassium, and water precisely formulated by the WHO. It exploits a biological mechanism that works even during severe diarrhoea — the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) in the intestinal lining, which continues to absorb sodium coupled to glucose even when other absorption mechanisms are failing. This allows ORS to actually replace fluids and electrolytes that are being lost through diarrhoea and vomiting. ORS is quite literally the most life-saving medical invention for diarrhoeal disease — it has prevented an estimated 1 million childhood deaths per year since its introduction. It is more important than any antibiotic, antidiarrhoeal, or other medication for most cases of gastroenteritis. In India, ORS sachets (branded as Electral, Nimwali, or generic ORS) are available at all chemists for a few rupees. The critical rules: always dissolve one sachet in EXACTLY 1 full litre of clean water; never add extra sugar or salt; give after every loose stool and vomiting episode.

faq.question: When should I give antibiotics for diarrhoea and when should I NOT?
faq.answer: Antibiotics are appropriate only in specific situations: (1) BLOODY DIARRHOEA (dysentery) — likely Shigella, Campylobacter, or amoeba — azithromycin for Shigella and Campylobacter in India; metronidazole/tinidazole for amoeba; (2) CHOLERA — all cases (azithromycin or doxycycline); (3) TYPHOID FEVER — azithromycin or ceftriaxone; (4) C. DIFFICILE — oral vancomycin; (5) TRAVELLER'S DIARRHOEA that is severe. When antibiotics are NOT appropriate and should NOT be given: (1) Viral gastroenteritis (90% of cases — antibiotics have zero effect against viruses); (2) Mild self-limiting watery diarrhoea in healthy adults; (3) STEC/bloody diarrhoea from E. coli O157:H7 — antibiotics dramatically increase the risk of HUS (kidney failure) — this is an absolute contraindication. In India, a very important point: Shigella and Campylobacter are now highly resistant to ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones) in many areas — azithromycin is the preferred antibiotic for these organisms, not ciprofloxacin.

faq.question: My 2-year-old has diarrhoea and vomiting — what should I do at home and when should I go to hospital?
faq.answer: The most important thing is giving ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) immediately — not plain water, not cola drinks, not sports drinks. ORS sachets from the chemist: dissolve 1 sachet in exactly 1 litre of boiled and cooled water. If your child is vomiting — give ORS very slowly, 5-10 mL (1-2 teaspoons) every 2-5 minutes by spoon or syringe. Even if they vomit, most of that small amount was absorbed. Continue breastfeeding if you are breastfeeding. Give 1 teaspoon of zinc (20 mg) daily for 10-14 days (government health centres provide this free). Avoid giving milk, formula, or solid food until vomiting has improved. WHEN TO GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY: your child has no wet nappy for 6+ hours; eyes are very sunken; mouth is bone dry with no saliva; child is not responding normally or very difficult to rouse; fever above 39°C; blood in the stool; refuses to take any ORS at all; vomiting is so severe that nothing stays down for more than 1-2 hours. Infants under 3 months with any vomiting or diarrhoea should be seen by a doctor the same day.

faq.question: What is C. difficile and why is it becoming a problem?
faq.answer: Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) is a bacterium that lives in the gut of some people without causing problems — but when antibiotics disrupt the normal protective gut bacteria, C. diff can overgrow and produce toxins that cause severe diarrhoea and colitis. The symptoms are frequent watery diarrhoea (3+ times daily), abdominal cramping, and sometimes fever, developing during or within 8 weeks of antibiotic use. C. diff is increasingly recognised in India as antibiotic use has increased dramatically. It is particularly dangerous in elderly patients in hospitals. Important facts: It forms spores that survive on surfaces for months — killed by bleach but NOT by alcohol hand sanitiser; handwashing with soap and water is essential for C. diff prevention. It should be treated with oral vancomycin (not IV vancomycin which doesn't reach the colon). The most effective treatment for repeat C. diff infections is Faecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) — now available at several major Indian hospitals — which cures >90% of recurrent cases.

faq.question: How can I prevent gastroenteritis during travel in India?
faq.answer: The five golden rules for safe travel in India: (1) DRINK SAFE WATER — bottled water (check seal is intact) or boiled water for drinking, brushing teeth, making ice; avoid tap water, well water, or drinks with ice of unknown source; (2) COOK IT or PEEL IT — eat food that is freshly cooked and served hot; peel fruits yourself; avoid pre-peeled, pre-cut, or pre-packaged fresh fruits from uncertain sources; (3) CHOOSE BUSY STREET FOOD STALLS with high turnover and food cooked fresh in front of you — high turnover means food is not sitting out; (4) WASH HANDS thoroughly with soap and water before eating and after using the toilet — always carry a small bar of soap; (5) AVOID RAW: raw salads, raw vegetables, raw shellfish, raw meat, unpasteurised dairy. Carry an ORS sachet, a zinc tablet (for children), and azithromycin for emergencies. The rotavirus, typhoid, and hepatitis A vaccines provide important additional protection — ensure your vaccinations are up to date before travel.

overview.description: Gastroenteritis is an acute inflammatory condition of the stomach and intestines characterised by diarrhoea (three or more loose or liquid stools per day), vomiting, nausea, and abdominal cramps — caused by infection with a broad range of viruses, bacteria, and parasites. It is one of the most common and universally experienced illnesses affecting people of all ages, in every country, in every socioeconomic class. Gastroenteritis is the second most common illness globally (after respiratory tract infections) and the second leading infectious cause of death in children under five years. The spectrum ranges from mild, self-limiting viral gastroenteritis resolving within 24-72 hours without treatment, to life-threatening acute watery diarrhoea (cholera), haemorrhagic colitis (Shiga toxin-producing E. coli — STEC), toxic megacolon (severe Clostridioides difficile), and invasive bacterial septicaemia. The most critical and immediately life-threatening consequence across all forms is dehydration — the excessive and rapid loss of water and electrolytes (particularly sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate) from vomiting and diarrhoea that can, if untreated, lead to hypovolaemic shock, acute kidney injury, cardiac arrhythmia, and death. Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) — the simple, inexpensive, lifesaving combination of glucose, sodium, and water — has saved tens of millions of lives globally since its development in the 1970s and remains the cornerstone of all gastroenteritis management regardless of causative agent. In India, diarrhoeal diseases cause over 300,000 deaths annually — predominantly in children under five years — making gastroenteritis prevention and management a national public health priority.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the small intestine and large intestine (colon); stomach; severe systemic infection affects kidneys (HUS), blood, brain, liver, and multiple organs
overview.prevalence: WHO estimates 1.7 billion cases of childhood diarrhoea globally per year; diarrhoeal diseases cause approximately 1.5 million deaths in children under five annually; approximately 15-20% of all childhood deaths globally; in India: diarrhoeal diseases are the second leading cause of under-5 mortality; approximately 300,000 deaths per year from diarrhoea; every Indian child has an average of 3-4 episodes of diarrhoea per year in the first five years of life
overview.age_group: All ages; highest morbidity and mortality in children under 5 years; second peak in elderly over 65 years; travellers and immunocompromised individuals at elevated risk for severe and unusual forms
overview.is_contagious_note: Most viral and bacterial gastroenteritis is highly contagious — spread by fecal-oral route, contaminated food and water, and direct person-to-person contact. Norovirus is extraordinarily contagious (only 18 viral particles required for infection); rotavirus, Shigella, and Clostridioides difficile also spread readily in close contact settings (households, healthcare facilities, schools)
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute gastroenteritis is by definition a short-term illness (days to weeks); however, some parasitic infections (Giardia, Entamoeba) and Clostridioides difficile can cause persistent or recurrent diarrhoea; post-infectious IBS (irritable bowel syndrome) can last months to years
overview.key_fact: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORS) has been described as 'potentially the most important medical advance of the 20th century' — a simple mixture of glucose, sodium, and water that exploits the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) to restore fluid and electrolyte balance even during severe diarrhoea. Approximately 1 million child deaths per year have been prevented by ORS since its introduction. Every caregiver and household should have ORS sachets and know how to prepare them correctly.

types.name: Viral Gastroenteritis
types.description: The most common cause of acute gastroenteritis globally — responsible for approximately 70-80% of all cases in high-income countries and a major proportion in developing countries. Viral gastroenteritis is invariably self-limiting in immunocompetent individuals; antibiotics have absolutely no role and should never be prescribed for viral gastroenteritis. The clinical presentation — explosive onset, vomiting predominant (particularly early), watery non-bloody diarrhoea, low-grade fever, and rapid resolution within 24-72 hours — strongly suggests a viral aetiology. Person-to-person and foodborne transmission are both important.

major_viruses.proportion: Most common cause of acute viral gastroenteritis in adults and older children globally; responsible for approximately 50% of all foodborne outbreak investigations
major_viruses.epidemiology: All year but winter peaks ('winter vomiting disease' in temperate climates; less seasonal in tropical India); all age groups; highly contagious in closed settings (cruise ships, hospitals, care homes, schools, military barracks); infective dose: only 18-100 viral particles — extraordinarily low; incubation: 12-48 hours
major_viruses.clinical_features: EXPLOSIVE onset of PROJECTILE VOMITING (dominant early symptom); watery non-bloody diarrhoea; abdominal cramping; low-grade fever (<38.5°C) or no fever; headache; myalgia; rapid complete recovery in 12-72 hours in immunocompetent adults; dehydration in elderly and young children
major_viruses.transmission: Fecal-oral; aerosol from vomiting (infectious radius up to 3 metres from vomiting episode — aerosolised viral particles settle on surfaces and are ingested); contaminated food (shellfish, salads, cold foods prepared by infected handlers); contaminated surfaces (survives on hard surfaces for weeks; resistant to many common disinfectants; requires >0.5 mg/L free chlorine or alcohol-based disinfectants)
major_viruses.treatment: SUPPORTIVE ONLY — ORS, antiemetics (ondansetron), rest; strict infection control; NO antibiotics (useless against viruses); recurrence possible (limited immunity — multiple serotypes)
major_viruses.infection_control: Exclude from work/school for 48 HOURS after LAST symptom (highly contagious); bleach (sodium hypochlorite 0.1% for surfaces — 1000 ppm) for cleaning; wash hands with soap and water (alcohol hand gel less effective against norovirus than soap and water for hand hygiene — important exception); healthcare setting outbreaks require strict cohorting and ward closure protocols
major_viruses.india_note: Norovirus outbreaks are underreported in India but increasingly recognised; commonly causes institutional outbreaks in schools, hospitals, and religious gatherings (pilgrimages — Kumbh Mela, Char Dham)

major_viruses.proportion: Leading cause of severe diarrhoeal disease and diarrhoea-related death in children under 5 globally; before vaccine introduction: caused 200,000+ childhood deaths annually worldwide
major_viruses.epidemiology: Peak incidence in infants and toddlers 3-24 months; cooler/dry season in tropical countries including India (October-March); develops in virtually all unvaccinated children by age 5; worldwide distribution; highly contagious
major_viruses.clinical_features: Onset: abrupt after 1-3 day incubation; VOMITING preceding diarrhoea by 1-2 days; PROFUSE WATERY diarrhoea (yellow-green colour; 10-20 stools per day); high fever (up to 39-40°C — higher than other viral gastroenteritis); rapid severe dehydration (within hours in infants); typical illness duration 5-7 days (longer than norovirus); rotavirus may cause seizures in febrile infants
major_viruses.transmission: Fecal-oral; person-to-person (very infectious — ID50 only 10 particles); fomites (survives on surfaces for days); respiratory droplet spread possible (explains winter seasonality)
major_viruses.treatment: SUPPORTIVE: ORS (early, aggressive); IV fluids if severe dehydration; zinc supplementation (WHO recommendation for children <5 — 20 mg/day for 10-14 days reduces duration and recurrence); ondansetron for vomiting facilitating ORS administration; breastfeeding continues; NO antibiotics
major_viruses.prevention: ROTAVIRUS VACCINE — the most important preventive intervention for childhood rotavirus gastroenteritis; included in India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) since 2016; 2-dose oral live attenuated vaccine (Rotarix) or 3-dose (RotaTeq); reduces hospitalisation for rotavirus diarrhoea by 85-95% in vaccinated cohorts; must complete series before 8 months of age
major_viruses.india_significance: Rotavirus causes approximately 25-30% of hospitalised acute diarrhoea in Indian children under 5 years; responsible for >78,000 child deaths in India annually (pre-vaccine era); nationwide Rotarix vaccination programme (Rotavac — indigenously developed by Bharat Biotech) has dramatically reduced childhood rotavirus hospitalisations in states with high coverage

major_viruses.proportion: Second most common cause of viral gastroenteritis in children under 2 years (after rotavirus); less common in adults
major_viruses.clinical_features: Longer incubation (8-10 days); prolonged watery diarrhoea lasting 5-12 days (longer than other viral gastroenteritis); vomiting less prominent than rotavirus; mild to absent fever; may persist as chronic diarrhoea in immunocompromised patients
major_viruses.treatment: Supportive; ORS; self-limiting in immunocompetent patients

major_viruses.proportion: 5-10% of viral gastroenteritis in children; peaks in winter
major_viruses.clinical_features: Mild watery diarrhoea; incubation 1-4 days; 2-4 day duration; milder than rotavirus; low-grade fever; spontaneous resolution

major_viruses.proportion: 30-40% of COVID-19 patients have GI symptoms
major_viruses.clinical_features: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea (watery); may precede or accompany respiratory symptoms; GI symptoms can be the primary COVID-19 presentation; isolated GI COVID without respiratory symptoms described
major_viruses.note: COVID-19 testing should be considered in patients with acute gastroenteritis during pandemic periods, particularly in high-risk contacts

types.name: Bacterial Gastroenteritis — Toxin-Mediated (Food Poisoning Syndromes)
types.description: Bacterial gastroenteritis caused by toxins produced by bacteria — either pre-formed in food (intoxication) or produced in the intestine after ingestion (toxico-infection). Characteristic feature: SHORT INCUBATION PERIOD (1-6 hours for pre-formed toxins in food) and vomiting-dominant presentation. Antibiotics are NOT indicated for most toxin-mediated bacterial gastroenteritis.

major_organisms.incubation: 1-6 hours (very short — toxin pre-formed in food)
major_organisms.foods: Potato/egg salads left at room temperature; sandwiches; cream pastries; deli meats; buffet foods
major_organisms.clinical_features: EXPLOSIVE VOMITING dominates; nausea; abdominal cramps; diarrhoea (may be mild); RARELY fever; short illness (6-24 hours); brief but very severe
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive — ORS; antiemetics; self-limiting; NO antibiotics needed (toxin-mediated)
major_organisms.note: Toxin is heat-stable — reheating food after contamination does NOT destroy it

major_organisms.subtypes: Two distinct syndromes: (1) Emetic (vomiting) syndrome — incubation 0.5-6 hours; from reheated rice/pasta; cereulide toxin; vomiting dominant; (2) Diarrhoeal syndrome — incubation 6-24 hours; enterotoxin produced in gut; diarrhoea dominant
major_organisms.foods: Reheated rice (fried rice left at room temperature), pasta, cooked cereals (emetic); meat products, sauces (diarrhoeal)
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive; self-limiting; NO antibiotics
major_organisms.india_note: Classic cause of food poisoning from reheated rice — common in dabbawala catered food, tiffin boxes left unrefrigerated; 'Chinese takeaway syndrome' equivalent

major_organisms.foods: Cooked meat, poultry, gravy kept warm; cafeteria and catered bulk food; institutional food
major_organisms.clinical_features: Watery diarrhoea + abdominal cramping; vomiting uncommon; no fever; brief (12-24 hours); usually self-limiting
major_organisms.treatment: Supportive; self-limiting

types.name: Bacterial Gastroenteritis — Invasive (Infectious Diarrhoea)
types.description: Bacterial gastroenteritis caused by invasive pathogens that infect and damage the intestinal mucosa — typically causing INFLAMMATORY diarrhoea (may be bloody or mucoid), fever, systemic illness, and elevated inflammatory markers. The diarrhoea may contain blood, mucus, and pus. Antibiotics are indicated in selected cases — particularly for dysentery (bloody diarrhoea with systemic illness), severe infection, and high-risk patients.

major_organisms.proportion: Most common bacterial cause of gastroenteritis in high-income countries; major cause in India
major_organisms.source: Undercooked poultry (most common); raw milk; contaminated water; contact with farm animals
major_organisms.clinical_features: Profuse watery or BLOODY diarrhoea; severe colicky abdominal cramps (may mimic appendicitis — Campylobacter ileitis); high fever (38-40°C); nausea and vomiting; illness lasts 2-10 days; MOST IMPORTANT COMPLICATION: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) — ascending paralysis occurring 2-6 weeks post-infection; most common identified trigger of GBS (20-40% of GBS follows Campylobacter)
major_organisms.treatment: Mild: supportive; Moderate-severe or immunocompromised: azithromycin 500 mg once daily × 3-5 days (first-line; ciprofloxacin resistance increasing — >50% resistance in some Indian settings); erythromycin alternative
major_organisms.public_health: Most cases are sporadic; outbreaks from contaminated poultry or water; raw chicken should never be washed (spreads Campylobacter around kitchen)

major_organisms.source: Undercooked poultry and eggs; raw meat; unpasteurised dairy; contaminated fruits and vegetables
major_organisms.clinical_features: Watery to mucoid diarrhoea; fever (38-40°C); abdominal cramps; nausea and vomiting; illness 4-7 days; BACTERAEMIA in 5-10% (particularly elderly, immunocompromised, infants, and those with sickle cell disease — seeding of bones/joints); REACTIVE ARTHRITIS post-infection
major_organisms.treatment: Mild: supportive; Severe/systemic/high-risk: ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 5-7 days or azithromycin (increasing Salmonella resistance to fluoroquinolones in India — send stool culture); IV antibiotics for bacteraemia
major_organisms.note: Antibiotics can prolong Salmonella faecal shedding in mild uncomplicated cases — reserve for severe or systemic disease

major_organisms.proportion: Leading cause of BLOODY diarrhoea (dysentery) in children globally; four species: S. dysenteriae (most virulent — associated with HUS), S. flexneri (most common in India), S. sonnei (most common in high-income countries), S. boydii
major_organisms.source: Contaminated water; person-to-person fecal-oral (extremely low infective dose — 10-100 organisms); food contaminated by infected handlers; flies
major_organisms.clinical_features: Initial watery diarrhoea progressing to DYSENTERY (bloody, mucoid diarrhoea with tenesmus — painful urge to defaecate); high fever (39-40°C); abdominal pain and cramps; prostration; Shiga toxin from S. dysenteriae type 1 can cause HUS (haemolytic uraemic syndrome); very common in Indian children under 5 years during monsoon season
major_organisms.treatment: Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD × 3-5 days (adults); Azithromycin 20 mg/kg/day × 3 days (children — preferred in India due to ciprofloxacin resistance in Shigella); ceftriaxone for severe disease; ORS essential
major_organisms.india_note: Shigella causes major outbreaks in India during monsoon season; associated with flooding, contaminated water supplies, poor sanitation; major cause of childhood dysentery deaths in rural India

major_organisms.organism: Enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) / Shiga Toxin-Producing E. coli (STEC) — particularly O157:H7
major_organisms.source: Undercooked ground beef (burgers); raw milk; raw leafy vegetables; contaminated water; person-to-person
major_organisms.clinical_features: BLOODY diarrhoea (prominent — frank blood and clots); severe abdominal cramps; ABSENT or LOW-GRADE fever (distinguishes from Shigella which has high fever); HUS develops in 5-10% of children — haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopaenia + acute renal failure occurring 5-10 days after onset
major_organisms.CRITICAL_WARNING: DO NOT GIVE ANTIBIOTICS for STEC O157:H7 — antibiotics (including fluoroquinolones) increase risk of HUS by 17-fold (lysing bacteria releases more Shiga toxin); DO NOT GIVE ANTIDIARRHOEALS (loperamide) — also increases HUS risk
major_organisms.treatment: SUPPORTIVE ONLY — aggressive IV fluid hydration; no antibiotics; no antidiarrhoeals; hospitalise any child with bloody diarrhoea for monitoring; check renal function, FBC, and urinalysis daily for HUS; nephrology if HUS develops

major_organisms.proportion: Most common cause of TRAVELLER'S DIARRHOEA globally
major_organisms.source: Contaminated food and water in developing countries (most commonly); the classic 'Delhi belly', 'Montezuma's revenge'
major_organisms.clinical_features: Watery (non-bloody) diarrhoea; abdominal cramps; nausea; mild fever or no fever; typically 3-5 days; self-limiting
major_organisms.treatment: ORS; azithromycin 1g single dose (traveller's diarrhoea in adults — most effective and most resistance-proof); ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily × 3 days (if azithromycin unavailable and resistance not a concern); rifaximin (non-absorbable antibiotic — for non-invasive traveller's diarrhoea in adults)

major_organisms.source: Contaminated water (the primary source — V. cholerae is a waterborne pathogen); raw shellfish; contaminated food
major_organisms.clinical_features: PROFUSE PAINLESS WATERY DIARRHOEA ('RICE WATER STOOLS' — pale, watery, containing mucus flecks, no blood); vomiting; RAPID EXTREME DEHYDRATION (can lose 10-20 litres of fluid per day); muscle cramps (from electrolyte loss); patient looks dehydrated, sunken eyes, 'washerwoman's hands'; no fever typically; death from dehydration within hours if untreated
major_organisms.treatment: EMERGENCY: AGGRESSIVE ORS is the priority — can save life within hours; Ringer's Lactate IV if severe dehydration; tetracycline 500 mg QID × 3 days (reduces duration and shedding) or azithromycin 1g single dose; doxycycline 300 mg single dose (adults); WHO cholera management protocol; case fatality <1% with prompt treatment vs >50% without
major_organisms.india_note: Endemic in India; seasonal outbreaks during monsoon flooding; Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal have highest incidence; part of WHO's 'Global Roadmap to Ending Cholera' — India committed to eliminating cholera by 2030

major_organisms.source: Undercooked pork; contaminated water; raw milk
major_organisms.clinical_features: Watery then bloody diarrhoea; fever; abdominal pain (RIGHT ILIAC FOSSA — mimics acute appendicitis — 'mesenteric adenitis' from Yersinia lymphadenopathy); particularly in children; post-infectious reactive arthritis; erythema nodosum
major_organisms.treatment: Mild: self-limiting; Severe: ciprofloxacin or doxycycline × 7-10 days; hospitalise for suspected appendicitis presentation

types.name: Parasitic Gastroenteritis
types.description: Parasitic intestinal infections causing gastroenteritis — typically producing more prolonged diarrhoea (weeks to months) compared to viral and bacterial gastroenteritis (days). Important causes in India given poor sanitation, contaminated water supplies, and overcrowding. Parasitic gastroenteritis is particularly important in: travellers returning from developing countries; immunocompromised patients; institutionalised populations; areas with poor water treatment.

major_organisms.proportion: Most common intestinal protozoal infection globally; endemic in India; 200 million cases/year worldwide
major_organisms.incubation: 1-3 weeks (long — distinguishes from most bacterial GE)
major_organisms.source: Contaminated water (cysts highly resistant to chlorination — major waterborne outbreak pathogen); person-to-person; food
major_organisms.clinical_features: Chronic WATERY or GREASY diarrhoea; malodorous sulphur/rotten egg burps (CHARACTERISTIC); bloating; abdominal distension; flatulence; weight loss; fatigue; NO blood or mucus in stool; persistent for weeks to months without treatment; MALABSORPTION (lactose intolerance from mucosal damage; fat malabsorption — steatorrhoea); particularly debilitating in children causing growth failure
major_organisms.diagnosis: Stool antigen test (ELISA or rapid immunochromatographic — sensitivity >90%); stool microscopy × 3 samples (cysts; 69% sensitivity single sample → 97% with 3 samples); duodenal biopsy (gold standard if stool tests negative but high suspicion)
major_organisms.treatment: Metronidazole 400 mg three times daily × 5-7 days (first-line in India — affordable, widely available); OR Tinidazole 2g SINGLE DOSE (equally effective, better tolerated, superior adherence — preferred); Nitazoxanide 500 mg BD × 3 days (alternative); treat all household contacts if multiple family members affected

major_organisms.proportion: 3rd leading parasitic cause of death globally (after malaria and schistosomiasis); highly prevalent in India
major_organisms.source: Contaminated water and food; fecal-oral; person-to-person (in endemic areas)
major_organisms.clinical_features: DYSENTERY — bloody, mucoid diarrhoea; tenesmus (painful incomplete feeling of bowel opening); abdominal cramping; fever (lower than Shigella); gradual onset; AMOEBIC LIVER ABSCESS (most common extraintestinal complication — right upper quadrant pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly; may occur weeks to months after intestinal infection — often without preceding diarrhoea); risk of perforation; toxic megacolon (rare)
major_organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy (trophozoites with ingested RBCs — pathognomonic; distinguish from non-pathogenic E. dispar — requires antigen testing or PCR for definitive distinction); Amoebic serology (IFA, ELISA) for liver abscess; Ultrasound for liver abscess
major_organisms.treatment: Intestinal: Metronidazole 500-750 mg three times daily × 5-10 days (kills trophozoites) FOLLOWED BY luminal agent — Diloxanide furoate 500 mg three times daily × 10 days OR Paromomycin 500 mg three times daily × 7 days (eliminates cysts — prevents relapse; critical step often forgotten); Liver abscess: Metronidazole 750 mg three times daily × 10 days ± image-guided percutaneous aspiration (abscesses >5 cm or not responding)
major_organisms.india_note: Amoebic dysentery is highly prevalent in India, particularly in areas with contaminated water supply, open defecation, and poor sanitation; during monsoon season outbreak peaks; the distinction between non-invasive E. dispar (non-pathogenic carrier) and pathogenic E. histolytica requires antigen tests — stool microscopy cannot distinguish morphologically

major_organisms.source: Contaminated water (oocysts are chlorine-resistant — major waterborne outbreak pathogen; requires filtration or UV for water treatment); person-to-person; contact with farm animals and pets
major_organisms.clinical_features: Profuse watery diarrhoea; abdominal cramps; nausea; low-grade fever; SELF-LIMITING in immunocompetent (1-2 weeks); SEVERE CHRONIC AND LIFE-THREATENING in AIDS (CD4 <50/mcL) — profuse, intractable, life-threatening diarrhoea that may not respond to any treatment; biliary cryptosporidiosis (cholangitis) in AIDS patients
major_organisms.diagnosis: Stool acid-fast staining (modified ZN stain — oocysts appear as bright red dots); stool antigen test; PCR
major_organisms.treatment: Immunocompetent: supportive; ORS; Nitazoxanide 500 mg twice daily × 3 days (limited evidence); Immunocompromised (HIV): Nitazoxanide has limited efficacy; only effective treatment is immune reconstitution with antiretroviral therapy (ART) — restore CD4 count

major_organisms.source: Contaminated fresh produce (raspberries, basil, snow peas); contaminated water; associated with imported fresh herbs and salads in outbreak settings
major_organisms.clinical_features: Watery non-bloody diarrhoea (may be profuse); prolonged (4-6 weeks untreated); fatigue; anorexia; weight loss; bloating; relapsing-remitting pattern
major_organisms.diagnosis: Stool modified acid-fast stain or autofluorescence microscopy; not detected on standard O&P stain — must specifically request Cyclospora testing
major_organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole) 160/800 mg twice daily × 7-10 days — drug of choice; ciprofloxacin alternative (less effective)

types.name: Clostridioides difficile (C. difficile) Colitis
types.description: Clostridioides difficile (formerly Clostridium difficile — C. diff) is an anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive bacterium that causes antibiotic-associated diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis — the most common healthcare-associated infectious diarrhoea globally. C. difficile colitis occurs when normal gut microbiota is disrupted by antibiotics, allowing C. difficile to overgrow and produce potent toxins (Toxin A — enterotoxin; Toxin B — cytotoxin; Binary toxin CDT in hypervirulent NAP1/BI/O27 strain). Not strictly a traditional gastroenteritis but increasingly important, particularly in hospitalised patients and the elderly.
risk_factors_specific: Recent antibiotic use — the single most important risk factor; ANY antibiotic can cause CDI but the highest risk antibiotics are: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin), clindamycin, broad-spectrum cephalosporins, and carbapenems
Age >65 years — impaired immune response; reduced gut microbiome diversity
Hospitalisation or nursing home residence — C. difficile spores persist on surfaces for months; colonised healthcare workers and patients are reservoirs
Proton pump inhibitors — reduce gastric acid barrier (allowing C. difficile spores to survive passage through stomach)
Previous C. difficile infection — 20-30% recurrence rate
clinical_spectrum: Mild CDI: watery diarrhoea (≥3 loose stools/day) without systemic features
Moderate CDI: diarrhoea + fever + abdominal pain; WBC elevated
Severe CDI: WBC >15,000; creatinine >50% rise; albumin <30 g/L; marked abdominal tenderness
Fulminant CDI: hypotension; toxic megacolon (colonic diameter >6 cm); ileus; perforation — ICU; mortality >50%
types.diagnosis: TOXIN TESTING of UNFORMED STOOL ONLY: (1) GDH (Glutamate Dehydrogenase) antigen test (screening — very sensitive but not specific); (2) Toxin A and B EIA (specific — confirms toxin production); (3) NAAT/PCR (most sensitive — detects toxin gene); (4) 2-step algorithm: GDH + Toxin EIA ± PCR; Colonoscopy: pseudomembranes (raised yellowish-white plaques on colonic mucosa) — pathognomonic
types.treatment: Stop precipitating antibiotic if possible; Mild-moderate: Oral Vancomycin 125 mg QID × 10 days (first-line) OR Fidaxomicin 200 mg twice daily × 10 days (preferred for first recurrence — lower recurrence rate); Metronidazole 400 mg three times daily × 10 days (now second-line; lower efficacy than vancomycin); Severe: Oral vancomycin 500 mg QID ± IV metronidazole; Fulminant: IV metronidazole + oral/rectal vancomycin; emergency colectomy for toxic megacolon; BEZLOTOXUMAB (monoclonal antibody against Toxin B — given with antibiotics to reduce recurrence in high-risk patients); Faecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) for recurrent CDI (2+ recurrences) — >90% efficacy; increasingly available in India
types.infection_control: Contact precautions (gown and gloves); side room (isolation); handwashing with SOAP AND WATER (alcohol gel does NOT kill C. difficile spores); bleach (sodium hypochlorite 1000 ppm) for environmental cleaning; do NOT use alcohol-based surface cleaners for C. difficile
types.india_note: C. difficile is increasingly recognised in Indian hospitals — rising antibiotic use (particularly fluoroquinolones and cephalosporins) is driving CDI; underdiagnosed due to limited testing; consider CDI in any hospitalised patient with diarrhoea on or within 8 weeks of antibiotics

types.name: Traveller's Diarrhoea
types.description: An acute gastroenteritis syndrome occurring in travellers visiting countries with different intestinal flora and sanitation standards. Defined as ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours during travel or within 10 days of return, with at least one associated symptom (abdominal cramps, nausea, vomiting, fever, tenesmus, or bloody stool). Affects 20-50% of international travellers to high-risk destinations (South and Southeast Asia, Africa, Mexico, Central America). India is both a high-risk destination for incoming travellers AND a significant source for Indians travelling within the country from low-risk urban areas to rural endemic regions.
types.causative_organisms: ETEC (40-70% — most common); EAEC (enteroaggregative E. coli — increasing recognition); Campylobacter (15-20%); Salmonella (5-15%); Shigella (5-10%); Norovirus (10-20% of all traveller's diarrhoea); Giardia and Cryptosporidium in prolonged or returning traveller's diarrhoea
types.grading: Mild (1-2 soft stools/day; tolerable symptoms — do not impair activities); Moderate (3-4 loose stools/day + distressing symptoms — partially impairs activities); Severe (≥4 loose stools/day + incapacitating symptoms OR dysentery — bloody stools, fever)
types.prevention: BOIL IT, COOK IT, PEEL IT, OR FORGET IT; bottled or purified water for drinking and ice; avoid raw salads, unpeeled fruit, and street food from uncertain sources; bismuth subsalicylate 2 tablets QID reduces risk by 65%; prophylactic antibiotics (rifaximin) for very short high-risk trips in immunocompromised — limited use in general due to resistance concerns
types.treatment: Mild: ORS + bismuth subsalicylate or loperamide (if non-bloody); Moderate-severe: Azithromycin 1g SINGLE DOSE (preferred globally — fewer resistance issues vs fluoroquinolones); ciprofloxacin alternative in non-SE Asia destinations (avoid in South/Southeast Asia — high fluoroquinolone resistance in ETEC and Campylobacter); rifaximin 200 mg three times daily × 3 days (non-absorbable — for non-invasive watery TD without fever or blood); DO NOT use loperamide with bloody diarrhoea or fever
types.when_to_seek_immediate_medical_attention: Bloody or mucoid diarrhoea; fever >38.5°C; severe dehydration; diarrhoea persisting >7 days; symptoms begin more than 10 days after return (consider parasitic causes — Giardia, Entamoeba)

types.name: Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhoea (Excluding C. difficile)
types.description: Diarrhoea directly caused by the antibiotic itself (not infection) — occurring in up to 30% of patients taking broad-spectrum antibiotics, particularly amoxicillin-clavulanate (co-amoxiclav), cephalosporins, and clindamycin. Mechanism: disruption of normal gut microbiota composition → altered colonic fermentation of carbohydrates → osmotic diarrhoea; direct stimulation of gut motility (erythromycin — motilin receptor agonist); altered bile salt metabolism. Usually watery, non-bloody, mild, and resolves when antibiotics stop. Treatment: probiotics (Saccharomyces boulardii, Lactobacillus GG) significantly reduce antibiotic-associated diarrhoea incidence; if severe or persistent → test for C. difficile.
types.management: Continue antibiotic if clinically necessary; probiotics reduce incidence by 50%; switch to alternative antibiotic if possible; test for C. difficile if diarrhoea severe, bloody, or persists after antibiotics stopped

severity_levels.name: Mild Gastroenteritis — No or Minimal Dehydration
severity_levels.description: Self-limiting gastroenteritis without significant dehydration. Safe for home management in healthy individuals.
severity_levels.criteria: Diarrhoea ≤5 loose stools per day; vomiting ≤2-3 episodes; able to tolerate oral fluids; no significant dehydration signs; urine output normal (pale yellow, regular frequency); no blood in stool; temperature <38.5°C or no fever; alert and fully oriented
severity_levels.dehydration_assessment: NO DEHYDRATION: normal skin turgor; moist mucous membranes; normal pulse and blood pressure; normal urine output; no excessive thirst; eyes not sunken; in infants — fontanelle not depressed; normal capillary refill (<2 seconds)
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unwell but ambulatory; able to stay at home; diet restricted but able to sip fluids
severity_levels.management: HOME management with ORS sachets (after every loose stool: 200-400 mL adult; 5-10 mL/kg child); continue breastfeeding in infants (NEVER STOP breastfeeding); advance to bland diet (khichdi, banana, rice) as tolerated; paracetamol for fever; NO antibiotics unless specific indication; zinc 20 mg/day × 10-14 days for children under 5 (WHO recommendation); return to GP if not improving at 48-72 hours
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Worsening dehydration; bloody stool appearing; temperature >38.5°C; inability to retain oral fluids; confusion in elderly

severity_levels.name: Moderate Gastroenteritis — Some Dehydration
severity_levels.description: Gastroenteritis with significant fluid losses and early-moderate dehydration requiring medical assessment and supervised oral or IV rehydration.
severity_levels.criteria: Diarrhoea >6 stools per day; vomiting preventing adequate oral intake; SOME DEHYDRATION: restless/irritable; thirsty; sunken eyes; mildly reduced skin turgor; dry mouth; mild tachycardia; reduced urine output (darker than normal); moderate fever 38.5-39.5°C; child lethargic but rousable
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to maintain adequate oral intake at home; requires medical attendance; may need IV fluids
severity_levels.management: Medical assessment — GP or urgent care; supervised oral rehydration with WHO ORS (50 mL/kg over 4 hours for moderate dehydration in children; 500 mL-1L over 2 hours in adults); if vomiting — ondansetron single oral dissolving tablet (facilitates ORS); IV fluids (Ringer's Lactate 20-30 mL/kg over 1 hour) if ORS fails; blood tests (electrolytes, renal function) if significant dehydration; stool culture if bacterial cause suspected (bloody stool, high fever, recent travel); antibiotic only for specific indications
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Haemodynamic instability; severe confusion; seizures; declining despite ORS and IV fluids

severity_levels.name: Severe Gastroenteritis — Severe Dehydration
severity_levels.description: Severe gastroenteritis with significant fluid and electrolyte losses requiring emergency hospital treatment and IV resuscitation.
severity_levels.criteria: SEVERE DEHYDRATION: sunken eyes and fontanelle (infants); very dry mouth and tongue; skin pinch returns very slowly (>2 seconds); very lethargic or unconscious; unable to drink; very reduced urine output or no urine for >8 hours; tachycardia (>120 bpm); hypotension; rapid weak pulse; cold extremities; temperature >39.5°C with rigor; bloody diarrhoea with fever
severity_levels.functional_impact: Complete incapacitation; risk of shock and organ failure; hospital admission mandatory
severity_levels.management: EMERGENCY: IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg over 3-4 hours (WHO Plan C for severe dehydration); immediate airway assessment; blood glucose (hypoglycaemia risk in children); electrolytes and renal function; stool cultures and blood cultures; antibiotics for specific bacterial causes; ICU-level monitoring for shock
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Septic shock — hypotension despite resuscitation; HUS (pallor, reduced urine, blood in urine 5-7 days after STEC diarrhoea); altered consciousness

severity_levels.name: Critical — Septic Shock, HUS, Toxic Megacolon
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening complications of severe gastroenteritis requiring ICU-level care.
severity_levels.examples: Cholera with extreme dehydration (>10L fluid loss/day) and cardiovascular collapse; STEC O157:H7 with HUS (haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopaenia + renal failure); Salmonella/Shigella bacteraemia and septic shock; Fulminant C. difficile colitis with toxic megacolon and perforation; Cholera in an infant with cardiac arrhythmia from hypokalaemia
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; IV fluid resuscitation targeting MAP >65 mmHg; vasopressors if refractory hypotension; IV broad-spectrum antibiotics for bacterial sepsis; dialysis (CRRT) for HUS-related AKI; platelet transfusion (HUS — controversial); emergency colectomy for toxic megacolon; continuous cardiac monitoring (hypokalaemia from cholera — arrhythmia risk)
severity_levels.mortality: Cholera without treatment: >50%; with treatment: <1%; HUS with good supportive care: 3-5% mortality; 25-30% long-term renal damage; Fulminant CDI with toxic megacolon: >50%

causative_agents_overview.viruses_70_80_percent: Dominant cause in high-income countries and increasingly recognised in India; norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus, astrovirus, sapovirus; self-limiting; antibiotics ineffective
causative_agents_overview.bacteria_15_20_percent: E. coli (multiple pathotypes), Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Vibrio cholerae, Clostridium difficile; may require antibiotics for specific organisms
causative_agents_overview.parasites_5_10_percent: Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica, Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora; cause more prolonged diarrhoea; specific antiparasitic treatment
causative_agents_overview.non_infectious: Functional diarrhoea; inflammatory bowel disease; lactose intolerance; coeliac disease — must be excluded in chronic presentations

routes_of_infection.description: Pathogens shed in stool of infected person → transferred to another person's mouth via contaminated hands, food, water, or surfaces. The fundamental route for all enteric pathogens.
routes_of_infection.chain_of_events: Infected person → stool contamination of hands → direct hand contact OR contamination of food/water/surfaces → ingestion by susceptible host → infection

routes_of_infection.description: Untreated or inadequately treated water containing enteric pathogens. Major route in India for Vibrio cholerae, Shigella, Giardia, Cryptosporidium, typhoid, and hepatitis A/E. Monsoon flooding contaminates wells and piped water supplies; intermittent water supply causes backflow contamination.
routes_of_infection.india_significance: Waterborne diarrhoeal outbreaks are extremely common in India during monsoon season; contamination of municipal water supplies is a recurrent problem; approximately 21% of communicable diseases in India are waterborne

routes_of_infection.description: Foods contaminated with pathogens through: improper storage temperatures (bacterial multiplication in the 'danger zone' 5-63°C); cross-contamination from raw to cooked food; infected food handlers; raw or undercooked foods (poultry, eggs, meat, shellfish); inadequate reheating.
routes_of_infection.high_risk_foods: Raw or undercooked poultry (Campylobacter, Salmonella); raw shellfish (Vibrio, HAV, norovirus); raw eggs (Salmonella); undercooked beef (STEC); unpasteurised dairy (Campylobacter, Listeria, Salmonella, STEC); street food left at room temperature; raw vegetables irrigated with contaminated water

routes_of_infection.description: Direct transmission from infected to uninfected person via hands, close contact, or sexual contact (anal-oral). Particularly important for: norovirus (touching surfaces contaminated with vomitus); rotavirus; Shigella (very low infective dose — 10-100 organisms); C. difficile (healthcare settings); Giardia (daycare centres, households).

risk_factors: Age under 5 years — immature immune system; lower gastric acid (less acid barrier); higher fluid requirement relative to body weight (dehydrate faster); smaller glycogen stores (hypoglycaemia risk); in India: malnutrition worsening severity
Age over 65 years — impaired immunity; multiple comorbidities; reduced thirst sensation; polypharmacy (PPIs reducing gastric acid barrier; antibiotics causing CDI)
Malnutrition — severe acute malnutrition dramatically worsens gastroenteritis severity and mortality; zinc deficiency impairs mucosal immunity
Lack of breastfeeding — breastmilk provides IgA, lactoferrin, oligosaccharides protecting against enteric infection; formula-fed infants have 5-10× higher risk of severe gastroenteritis
No access to safe water — rural India: well water, surface water, or intermittent piped water supply greatly increases risk

Poor sanitation and open defecation — 40-50% of rural India still lacks access to adequate sanitation; open defecation (though dramatically reduced by Swachh Bharat Mission) remains a major faecal-oral transmission driver
Overcrowded living conditions — facilitates person-to-person spread of norovirus, rotavirus, and Shigella
Low socioeconomic status — compounding effect of poor water, sanitation, hygiene (WASH), and nutrition
International travel — high-risk destinations (South Asia, Africa, Southeast Asia, Latin America); change in gut flora; exposure to new pathogens
Antibiotic use — disrupts protective gut microbiota; predisposes to C. difficile; selects resistant organisms

Proton pump inhibitor (PPI) use — reduces gastric acid barrier (normally kills most ingested pathogens); significantly increases risk of foodborne gastroenteritis including Salmonella, Campylobacter, and C. difficile
Immunosuppression — HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, transplantation, biologic therapy — more severe disease; unusual organisms (Cryptosporidium, cytomegalovirus colitis, atypical Salmonella)
Inflammatory bowel disease — barrier dysfunction; altered gut flora; increased susceptibility to enteric infection and C. difficile
Unvaccinated children (not received rotavirus vaccine) — dramatically higher risk of severe rotavirus gastroenteritis

symptoms.overview: Gastroenteritis symptoms depend critically on the causative agent, the portion of gut involved, the patient's age and immune status, and the infectious dose. The THREE KEY DIFFERENTIATING QUESTIONS are: (1) Is there blood in the stool? — BLOODY diarrhoea (dysentery) suggests invasive bacteria (Shigella, Campylobacter, STEC) or Entamoeba and changes management; (2) Is there high fever? — high fever (>39°C) with diarrhoea suggests invasive bacterial infection; absent/low fever with vomiting suggests viral or toxin-mediated; (3) How quickly did it start and how long has it lasted? — onset within 6 hours after food suggests preformed toxin (Staph, B. cereus); 6-72 hours suggests bacterial infection; weeks suggest parasitic infection.

primary_symptoms.name: Diarrhoea — Character is Diagnostically Critical
primary_symptoms.description: The cardinal symptom — defined as ≥3 loose or liquid stools per 24 hours (compared with the person's normal stool habit). The CHARACTER of the diarrhoea is the most important diagnostic clue: WATERY diarrhoea (no blood, no mucus) = non-invasive: viral gastroenteritis, ETEC, Cholera (rice-water stools), Giardia, Cryptosporidium; BLOODY diarrhoea (dysentery — blood ± mucus ± pus in stool) = invasive: Shigella, Campylobacter, STEC, Entamoeba histolytica, C. difficile; GREASY, FOUL-SMELLING, FLOATING stools = Giardia (fat malabsorption — steatorrhoea); MUCOID stool = Shigella, Entamoeba, IBS exacerbation; LARGE VOLUME, PALE, WATERY = Cholera, Cryptosporidium; RICE-WATER APPEARANCE = Cholera (pathognomonic).
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Life-threatening depending on volume and duration
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: BLOOD IN DIARRHOEA is an ALARM FEATURE — requires investigation; NEVER give antidiarrhoeals (loperamide) for bloody diarrhoea; suspect STEC — do NOT give antibiotics without culture result

primary_symptoms.name: Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Protective mechanism to eliminate toxins and pathogens. In VIRAL gastroenteritis (norovirus especially): vomiting is EXPLOSIVE and PROJECTILE — often the first and dominant symptom; may precede diarrhoea by several hours; vomiting is more severe than in bacterial gastroenteritis. In FOOD POISONING (Staph toxin): vomiting begins within 1-6 hours of eating — profuse; may be explosive. In most bacterial gastroenteritis: diarrhoea predominates over vomiting. In CHOLERA: vomiting is present but diarrhoea is dramatically more severe. Vomiting prevents adequate oral fluid replacement — the key clinical problem; if vomiting prevents ORS intake, IV fluids or antiemetic pre-treatment with ondansetron are required.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Persistent vomiting preventing oral hydration = indication for IV fluids or ondansetron administration

primary_symptoms.name: Abdominal Cramps and Pain
primary_symptoms.description: Colicky, diffuse, periumbilical or generalised abdominal pain from intestinal hyperperistalsis as the inflamed gut attempts to expel its contents. In most gastroenteritis, pain is cramplike and comes in waves. SEVERE, CONSTANT, LOCALISED abdominal pain (particularly right iliac fossa — Yersinia, Campylobacter ileitis mimicking appendicitis) or generalised peritonism should raise concern for complications. In C. difficile: cramping abdominal pain with extreme tenderness — check for toxic megacolon (abdominal distension, absent bowel sounds).
primary_symptoms.note: Severe constant non-colicky pain with rigidity = perforation or toxic megacolon — SURGICAL EMERGENCY

primary_symptoms.name: Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Fever is a key discriminator between viral, bacterial (invasive), and toxin-mediated gastroenteritis. ABSENT OR LOW-GRADE fever (<38°C): viral gastroenteritis (most common), toxin-mediated food poisoning (Staph, B. cereus — typically no fever); LOW-GRADE TO MODERATE fever (38-39°C): most bacterial gastroenteritis (Salmonella, Campylobacter), rotavirus; HIGH FEVER (>39-40°C): Shigella, severe Campylobacter, Salmonella bacteraemia, cholangitis, amoebic liver abscess; FEVER WITH RIGORS in gastroenteritis = bacteraemia — urgent blood cultures and IV antibiotics.

primary_symptoms.name: Dehydration Signs — The Most Critical Clinical Assessment
primary_symptoms.description: Dehydration from fluid and electrolyte losses in gastroenteritis is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality. Assessment of dehydration severity guides the urgency and route of treatment. SIGNS OF DEHYDRATION by system: Eyes: sunken (most visible in infants); Mouth: dry lips and tongue; Skin: reduced turgor (skin pinch recoils slowly when pinched — in severe dehydration, skin 'tents' and stays folded for >2 seconds); Heart: tachycardia (compensatory); Blood pressure: normal then low (late sign — indicates shock); Urine: reduced volume, darker colour, concentrated (normal = pale yellow; mild dehydration = yellow; moderate = amber; severe = no urine); Fontanelle: sunken (infants — important clinical sign); Consciousness: initially irritable and restless → lethargic → obtunded (severe dehydration/shock).

dehydration_classification.no_dehydration: <3% body weight — normal eyes, mouth, skin turgor, pulse, blood pressure, urine; manage at home with ORS after each loose stool
dehydration_classification.some_dehydration: 3-9% — restless, thirsty, sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced skin turgor, fast heart rate; ORS 75 mL/kg over 4 hours
dehydration_classification.severe_dehydration: >10% — very sunken eyes, no tears, very dry mouth, very poor skin turgor, very fast weak pulse, hypotension, little or no urine, lethargic or unconscious; IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg immediately

primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Dehydration assessment is the most important clinical skill in managing gastroenteritis — it determines the urgency and route of rehydration

secondary_symptoms: Headache — from fever, systemic viral illness, dehydration
Myalgia (muscle aches) — particularly in viral gastroenteritis (norovirus, rotavirus); cytokine-mediated systemic response
Malaise and fatigue — universal; may persist for weeks post-infection
Loss of appetite — common with all forms of gastroenteritis
Tenesmus — persistent feeling of needing to defaecate despite empty rectum; painful; characteristic of DYSENTERY (Shigella, Entamoeba, STEC, C. difficile colitis)
Excessive thirst — compensatory mechanism in dehydration; important marker of dehydration in children
Sulphur/rotten egg burps — characteristic of Giardia infection
Bloating and abdominal distension — Giardia, post-gastroenteritis functional bowel
Weight loss — in protracted or parasitic gastroenteritis; nutritional deficit particularly in malnourished children
symptoms_in_children: Infants and young children present differently — they CANNOT describe their symptoms; clinical assessment relies on: behaviour (irritable, crying, lethargic), appearance (sunken eyes, sunken fontanelle in infants <18 months, dry mouth, no tears when crying), urine (no wet nappies for 6+ hours), feeding (refusing to drink or breastfeed)

Febrile seizures — children aged 6 months to 6 years can develop febrile convulsions with high temperatures from gastroenteritis (particularly rotavirus — even higher fever than bacterial); manage seizure; fever control; do NOT give antiepileptics for simple febrile seizure

Rotavirus diarrhoea in infants: characteristically begins with 1-2 days of vomiting BEFORE diarrhoea; high fever (38-40°C); watery yellow-green diarrhoea; becomes dehydrated very rapidly (infants have larger proportional fluid requirements and smaller reserves)

Post-infectious lactose intolerance: very common in children after viral gastroenteritis (particularly rotavirus and Giardia damage intestinal brush border causing temporary lactase deficiency) → secondary lactose intolerance → worsening diarrhoea when milk reintroduced; avoid milk for 5-7 days; plain yogurt is usually tolerated (bacteria produce lactase)
Return to nursery/school: 48 hours after LAST episode of vomiting or diarrhoea
warning_signs_requiring_urgent_attention: BLOOD IN STOOL — bloody or mucoid diarrhoea at any age; possible dysentery (Shigella), STEC, C. difficile, amoebic colitis; requires prompt medical evaluation
Signs of SEVERE DEHYDRATION — no urination >8 hours; very sunken eyes; no tears; unable to drink; limp and unresponsive infant; hypotension in adults — EMERGENCY
HIGH FEVER >39°C WITH DIARRHOEA — possible invasive bacterial infection, bacteraemia, or severe systemic illness
CONFUSION or ALTERED CONSCIOUSNESS — possible dehydration shock; hyponatraemia (if given plain water without electrolytes); or severe systemic infection
VOMITING FOR >24 HOURS PREVENTING ANY FLUID INTAKE — risk of severe dehydration
DIARRHOEA NOT IMPROVING after 72 hours in adults or 24 hours in infants (<6 months)
PALLOR and REDUCED URINE OUTPUT 5-7 days after a bloody diarrhoeal illness — POSSIBLE HUS (Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome) from STEC — EMERGENCY
INFANT UNDER 3 MONTHS WITH GASTROENTERITIS — always requires immediate medical assessment (very limited reserves; extremely rapid deterioration)
IMMUNOCOMPROMISED PATIENT with any gastroenteritis — HIV, chemotherapy, transplant — higher risk of severe invasive disease and unusual organisms

medical_history: Duration of illness — when did it start; days vs weeks (acute bacterial/viral vs parasitic)
Stool character — watery vs bloody vs mucoid; colour; odour; quantity per day; 'rice-water' appearance (cholera)
Symptom sequence — vomiting then diarrhoea (viral, Staph toxin) vs diarrhoea then bloody diarrhoea (Shigella, Campylobacter); vomiting without diarrhoea (early Staph toxin)
Fever — degree and duration; rigors (bacteraemia); temperature peak

Dietary history — specific foods consumed in preceding 72 hours; exact timing of food ingestion relative to symptom onset (INCUBATION PERIOD — critical diagnostic clue; <6 hours = toxin; 6-24 hours = bacterial; 1-5 days = invasive bacteria; 1-3 weeks = parasitic)
Water source — tap (municipal), well, river, spring, bottled; water treatment (boiled, filtered, chlorinated)
Travel history — recent travel; where; duration; local food and water; same region travel in India (rural travel within high-risk states)
Contacts — other ill household members or colleagues who ate the same food; community outbreak investigation; healthcare worker with patient contact
Recent antibiotic use — type; timing; duration; C. difficile risk
Hospitalisation history — recent healthcare exposure (C. difficile risk)
PPI or acid suppression medication — increases susceptibility to foodborne pathogens

Medical history — inflammatory bowel disease (gastroenteritis can trigger IBD flare; IBD mimics infectious gastroenteritis); immunosuppression; HIV status; sickle cell disease (Salmonella osteomyelitis risk); haemolytic anaemia (pigment stones — gallstone complication risk)
Vaccination history — rotavirus vaccine (children); typhoid; hepatitis A; cholera
Occupation — healthcare worker (C. difficile exposure; occupational exclusion requirements); food handler (public health mandatory exclusion); childcare worker
Breastfeeding status — breastfed infants generally have less severe gastroenteritis; management continues breastfeeding
physical_examination: HYDRATION STATUS — the single most important examination finding in gastroenteritis management; assess systematically:
Eyes: sunken (significant dehydration); tears present when crying (absent in moderate-severe dehydration); normal eye position vs sunken
Mouth and tongue: moisture — wet vs moist vs dry vs 'bone dry' (severe dehydration)
Skin: turgor — pinch abdominal or thigh skin; release — normal recoil <1 second; slow recoil 1-2 seconds = some dehydration; very slow 'skin tenting' >2 seconds = severe dehydration

Fontanelle (infants <18 months): palpate anterior fontanelle with infant in upright position; normal = soft and flat; SUNKEN = moderate-severe dehydration; BULGING = increased intracranial pressure (meningitis — different diagnosis)

Vital signs: heart rate (tachycardia — most sensitive early indicator of hypovolaemia); blood pressure (normal until severe dehydration; then hypotension — late, alarming sign); temperature; respiratory rate (tachypnoea in metabolic acidosis from severe diarrhoea — Kussmaul breathing); pulse character (full and bounding vs weak and thready)
Capillary refill time: press fingernail for 5 seconds; normal refill <2 seconds; delayed >3 seconds = poor perfusion
Urine colour: pale yellow = well hydrated; yellow = mild dehydration; dark yellow/amber = moderate dehydration; absent = severe dehydration

Abdominal examination: distension (toxic megacolon — C. difficile; obstruction); tenderness (diffuse in most gastroenteritis; localised RIF in Yersinia/Campylobacter ileitis; RUQ in cholecystitis differential); bowel sounds (hyperactive = active gastroenteritis; absent = ileus/toxic megacolon — SERIOUS); guarding/rigidity = peritonitis/perforation — EMERGENCY
Rectal examination: if indicated — blood on glove (confirms bloody diarrhoea); mucus; rectal tenderness; mass (exclude IBD, cancer, intussusception in children)

Signs of specific complications: pallor and bruising = possible HUS (after E. coli diarrhoea); jaundice = HAV; periumbilical/flank bruising = haemorrhagic pancreatitis; purpura = meningococcal septicaemia (important differential for ill child)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Culture and Sensitivity (MC&S) — Midstream or Fresh Stool Sample
diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard investigation for identifying specific bacterial pathogens in gastroenteritis. Fresh stool (or rectal swab if stool cannot be obtained) is plated on selective culture media to grow and identify Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, E. coli, Yersinia, and Vibrio; antimicrobial sensitivities are tested to guide antibiotic choice. Sensitivity: 50-70% depending on pathogen and timing — best yield within first 48-72 hours of illness, before antibiotic initiation.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify bacterial pathogens; guide antibiotic selection; public health surveillance; outbreak investigation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Specific bacterial growth = bacteria confirmed; sensitivity results guide antibiotic choice; stool culture takes 48-72 hours for results
diagnostic_tests.when_to_send: Bloody diarrhoea; fever >38.5°C with diarrhoea; severe or protracted illness; returning traveller; immunocompromised patient; suspected outbreak; hospitalised patients with diarrhoea; food handler or healthcare worker
diagnostic_tests.india_note: MUST be sent BEFORE starting antibiotics; E. coli sensitivity patterns vary widely across India — local antibiogram essential for empirical antibiotic choice; Shigella fluoroquinolone resistance is 60-80% in some Indian centres — azithromycin preferred empirically for Shigella in India

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Multiplex PCR Panel (GI Pathogen Panel)
diagnostic_tests.description: Simultaneous PCR detection of 20+ bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens from a single stool sample — returning results in 2-6 hours versus 48-72 hours for culture. Dramatically higher sensitivity (>90% for most pathogens) and speed compared to traditional culture. Detects: bacteria (Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, STEC, Yersinia, Vibrio); viruses (norovirus, rotavirus, adenovirus, astrovirus, sapovirus); parasites (Giardia, Cryptosporidium, Entamoeba, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora). Examples: BioFire FilmArray GI Panel; Luminex xTAG GI Pathogen Panel.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid comprehensive diagnosis; guide appropriate antibiotic and antiparasitic therapy; infection control decisions; severely ill patients; immunocompromised; outbreak investigation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Detects most common pathogens simultaneously; results in 2-6 hours; sensitivity >90% for included pathogens
diagnostic_tests.india_note: Available at major urban diagnostic centres and referral hospitals in India; cost-effective for severe illness where rapid diagnosis changes management; gradually becoming more widely available

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Stool Microscopy for Ova, Cysts, and Parasites (OCP)
diagnostic_tests.description: Light microscopy examination of stool for protozoan cysts, trophozoites, and helminth eggs. Essential for diagnosing Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica/dispar, Cryptosporidium (requires special Modified Acid-Fast / Ziehl-Neelsen staining — MUST request specifically), Cyclospora (also requires modified acid-fast stain), and intestinal helminths. Three separate stool samples collected on different days significantly improves sensitivity (intermittent cyst shedding: single sample 69% sensitive for Giardia; 3 samples → 97%).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect parasitic intestinal infection in prolonged diarrhoea (>7-14 days); returning travellers; immunocompromised; children in endemic areas with persistent diarrhoea
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Giardia cysts or trophozoites; Entamoeba trophozoites with ingested RBCs (pathognomonic of E. histolytica invasion); acid-fast oocysts (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora); helminth ova
diagnostic_tests.note: Entamoeba histolytica and E. dispar are morphologically identical on microscopy — cannot be distinguished without antigen testing or PCR; important for guiding treatment

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Rapid Antigen Tests — Point of Care
diagnostic_tests.description: Rapid immunochromatographic tests providing results in 15-30 minutes for specific pathogens:
available_tests: Giardia stool antigen ELISA or rapid test — sensitivity >90%; gold standard for non-microscopy Giardia diagnosis
Rotavirus stool antigen — widely available; rapid 15-30 minute test; seasonal diagnosis and outbreak confirmation
Norovirus stool antigen — less sensitive than PCR but useful in outbreak settings
C. difficile GDH antigen + Toxin A/B EIA — 2-step testing algorithm for CDI
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid diagnosis at point of care; guide treatment decisions; infection control decisions; outbreak confirmation
diagnostic_tests.india_availability: Rotavirus and Giardia antigen tests widely available; C. difficile testing increasingly available at large urban hospitals

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) and Inflammatory Markers (CRP, Procalcitonin)
diagnostic_tests.description: Blood tests to assess severity of infection and guide antibiotic decisions. Leucocytosis with neutrophilia indicates significant bacterial infection. Leucopenia may occur in typhoid fever (relative bradycardia + leucopenia is characteristic). Lymphocytosis suggests viral aetiology. Thrombocytopaenia in combination with microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia and rising creatinine = HUS triad (STEC complication). CRP elevated in bacterial more than viral; procalcitonin >0.5 ng/mL suggests bacterial bacteraemia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Distinguish bacterial from viral infection; detect HUS (falling platelets, falling Hb, rising creatinine); assess severity; guide antibiotic decisions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: WBC >15,000 with neutrophilia: bacterial infection; Lymphocytosis: viral or typhoid; Thrombocytopenia + low Hb + rising creatinine = HUS screen urgently; CRP >50 mg/L: significant bacterial infection; Procalcitonin >0.5: bacteraemia

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Electrolytes, Renal Function, and Blood Glucose
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in moderate-severe gastroenteritis. HYPONATRAEMIA is critically dangerous in infants and young children — paradoxically common when well-meaning caregivers give PLAIN WATER without electrolytes (water dilutes sodium further — worse than giving nothing; can cause cerebral oedema and seizures — the 'water intoxication' danger with plain water in infants); always use ORS. HYPOKALAEMIA from diarrhoea causes muscle weakness and cardiac arrhythmia. ELEVATED CREATININE indicates AKI — either from dehydration (pre-renal) or HUS (intrinsic renal). HYPOGLYCAEMIA in young children from fasting and depleted glycogen stores — common; requires immediate glucose correction.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess electrolyte disturbances; detect AKI; detect hypoglycaemia (children); guide IV fluid composition; diagnose hyponatraemia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Na <135: hyponatraemia; Na <125: dangerous — seizure risk; K+ <3.5: hypokalaemia — supplement; Creatinine rising: AKI; Glucose <3.5 mmol/L (children): hypoglycaemia — treat immediately
diagnostic_tests.critical_warning: NEVER give plain water alone to a severely dehydrated infant — this worsens hyponatraemia; always use WHO ORS which contains the correct sodium concentration

diagnostic_tests.test_name: C. difficile Toxin Testing (EIA and GDH Antigen)
diagnostic_tests.description: TWO-STEP ALGORITHM recommended: (1) GDH (Glutamate Dehydrogenase) antigen ELISA — highly sensitive screening test (detects all C. difficile, including non-toxin-producing strains); THEN (2) If GDH positive: Toxin A and B EIA (confirms toxin production — the toxins that cause disease); or (3) NAAT (PCR for toxin genes — most sensitive confirmatory test). This 2-step approach maximises sensitivity while maintaining specificity. ONLY test UNFORMED/LIQUID STOOL — formed stool in an asymptomatic patient should NOT be tested (high false-positive colonisation rate).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose C. difficile infection (CDI) in patients on or recently on antibiotics; hospitalised patients with diarrhoea; patients >65 years with diarrhoea
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: GDH positive + Toxin EIA positive = CDI confirmed; GDH positive + Toxin EIA negative + PCR positive = possible CDI (carrier vs infection — treat if clinically appropriate); GDH negative = CDI very unlikely
diagnostic_tests.testing_pitfalls: Do NOT test formed stool; do NOT test stool from patients only on laxatives; only test patients with ≥3 unformed stools in 24 hours

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Blood Culture
diagnostic_tests.description: Two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic) before antibiotics in all patients with: fever >39°C with severe illness; rigors; signs of systemic sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion); immunocompromised patients; infants under 3 months; elderly patients with severe gastroenteritis. Positive in 5-10% of bacterial gastroenteritis — particularly Salmonella (bacteraemia more common), Shigella (rare), Campylobacter (rare), and STEC (do NOT give antibiotics if blood culture shows STEC — increases HUS risk).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect bacteraemia; guide systemic antibiotic therapy; detect unusual pathogens in immunocompromised
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive blood culture = bacteraemia; Salmonella in blood culture = systemic Salmonellosis — IV antibiotics; results 24-72 hours

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Urinalysis and Urine Microscopy
diagnostic_tests.description: HAEMATURIA and PROTEINURIA in a child with bloody diarrhoea from STEC infection are critical HUS screening markers. Red cell casts on urine microscopy confirm intrinsic renal involvement (glomerular). Urinalysis also helps assess hydration status (concentrated urine in dehydration) and excludes urinary tract infection mimicking abdominal gastroenteritis symptoms.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for HUS (haematuria, proteinuria, RBC casts) in STEC diarrhoea; assess hydration; exclude UTI; monitor renal function in severe gastroenteritis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Haematuria + proteinuria + red cell casts + falling urine output after STEC diarrhoea = HUS — PAEDIATRIC NEPHROLOGY EMERGENCY

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Sigmoidoscopy / Colonoscopy (Selected Cases)
diagnostic_tests.description: Not required for uncomplicated gastroenteritis. Indicated in: suspected C. difficile colitis when stool testing inconclusive (pseudomembranes visible on colonoscopy = pathognomonic); distinguishing infectious colitis from inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) exacerbation; chronic bloody diarrhoea not resolving; immunocompromised patients with unexplained severe diarrhoea (CMV colitis, Kaposi's sarcoma, mycobacterial colitis in AIDS).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose C. difficile pseudomembranous colitis; distinguish IBD from infectious colitis; diagnose unusual colitis in immunocompromised

medicines.note: The cornerstone of ALL gastroenteritis management is ORAL REHYDRATION THERAPY (ORT) — regardless of cause, age, or severity. Most gastroenteritis is self-limiting and does NOT require antibiotics. Antibiotics are indicated for specific bacterial and parasitic infections but should NEVER be given empirically for all gastroenteritis — this drives resistance and can cause harm (e.g., antibiotics for STEC increase HUS risk).
