The decision to use antibiotics should be based on the clinical picture (severity, bloody diarrhoea, fever), stool culture results when available, and local resistance patterns.
treatment_principles: 1. REHYDRATION IS THE MOST CRITICAL AND UNIVERSAL TREATMENT — ORS should be started immediately for any gastroenteritis; no other treatment is as important or life-saving

2. CONTINUE FEEDING — early refeeding (within 4-6 hours of starting rehydration) promotes intestinal mucosal recovery; the outdated 'rest the gut' fasting approach prolongs illness; breastfeeding MUST CONTINUE in infants
3. ANTIBIOTICS: DO NOT give empirical antibiotics for ALL gastroenteritis; indications are specific — see below; antibiotic overuse is a leading driver of antimicrobial resistance globally
4. DO NOT GIVE ANTIBIOTICS FOR STEC (EHEC O157:H7) — antibiotic treatment significantly increases HUS risk (17-fold); supportive treatment only
5. DO NOT GIVE ANTIDIARRHOEALS (loperamide) for: bloody diarrhoea; fever >38.5°C with diarrhoea; children under 2 years; suspected STEC; C. difficile; invasive bacterial colitis
6. ZINC SUPPLEMENTATION for children under 5 years with diarrhoea (WHO recommendation): 20 mg/day for 10-14 days — reduces severity, duration, and risk of recurrence
7. ANTIEMETICS (ondansetron): evidence-based use in children with vomiting and gastroenteritis — single oral dissolving dose significantly reduces hospitalisation by enabling ORS administration
8. PROBIOTICS: Saccharomyces boulardii and Lactobacillus GG reduce diarrhoea duration by approximately 24 hours; recommended adjunct during and after antibiotic courses

categories.category_name: Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) — THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT TREATMENT
categories.purpose: Replace fluids and electrolytes lost through diarrhoea and vomiting using the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) mechanism — which remains functional during diarrhoea unlike passive sodium absorption. WHO ORS has saved tens of millions of lives globally and is the cornerstone of all gastroenteritis management.
categories.who_ors_composition: Sodium 75 mmol/L; Chloride 65 mmol/L; Glucose 75 mmol/L; Potassium 20 mmol/L; Citrate 10 mmol/L; Osmolarity 245 mOsm/L (reduced osmolarity ORS — superior to original high-osmolarity formulation; reduces stool output and vomiting; fewer treatment failures)

medicines.name: WHO Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) — Reduced Osmolarity
medicines.form: Powder sachet (dissolve 1 sachet in 1 litre of clean water — NOT less water; DO NOT add extra sugar or salt)

dosage.no_dehydration_prevention: Adults: 200-400 mL after EACH loose stool; Children: 50-100 mL after each loose stool; Infants (<2 years): 50-100 mL after each loose stool (administer by spoon or syringe — 5-10 mL every 2-5 minutes if vomiting); continue until diarrhoea resolves
dosage.some_dehydration_rehydration: Adults: 500-1000 mL over 2-4 hours; Children: 75 mL/kg over 4 hours; Infants: 75 mL/kg over 4 hours; reassess dehydration at 4 hours
dosage.severe_dehydration: IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg first (Plan C); switch to ORS as soon as can drink

medicines.mechanism: SGLT1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter type 1) on intestinal enterocyte brush border is unaffected by diarrhoea-causing enterotoxins — it continues to transport sodium coupled to glucose into the cell (1:1 ratio), carrying water by osmosis; this is why glucose-sodium ORS works even in severe secretory diarrhoea (cholera) where intestinal electrolyte transport is otherwise maximally disrupted
critical_instructions: ALWAYS dissolve in EXACTLY 1 litre of water — not 500 mL (makes hypertonic solution which worsens dehydration)
Use CLEAN WATER — boiled and cooled water is best; filtered or bottled water acceptable; NEVER use untreated river, well, or tap water in areas with water contamination
NEVER add extra sugar, salt, or other substances to ORS — alters the critical electrolyte balance
NEVER dilute ORS with extra water
Prepared ORS solution should be used within 24 hours — discard unused portion
If ORS sachets unavailable: home sugar-salt solution — 1 level teaspoon salt + 8 level teaspoons sugar in 1 litre clean water (emergency only — less precise than WHO ORS)
medicines.vomiting_management: If patient vomits — CONTINUE ORS but in SMALL SIPS (5-10 mL every 2-5 minutes by spoon or syringe in children); most vomiting patients can retain fluid given very slowly; allow 10 minutes rest then restart; do NOT stop ORS after vomiting
medicines.who_recommendation: WHO Essential Medicine; first-line treatment for diarrhoeal disease of any cause globally; endorsed by WHO, UNICEF, and all major global health organisations

medicines.name: Intravenous Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's Solution) — Severe Dehydration
medicines.dosage: SEVERE DEHYDRATION (WHO Plan C): Children: 100 mL/kg IV Ringer's Lactate over 3 hours (infants <12 months: first 30 mL/kg over 1 hour, then 70 mL/kg over 2 hours); Adults: 1-2 litres Ringer's Lactate rapidly IV (over 30-60 minutes initially); reassess every 30-60 minutes; continue until rehydrated then SWITCH TO ORAL ORS
medicines.use_case: Severe dehydration not manageable orally; inability to take oral fluids (severe vomiting, unconsciousness, paralytic ileus); severe cholera; infants with >10% dehydration
medicines.preferred_over_normal_saline: Ringer's Lactate preferred over 0.9% Normal Saline for large volume resuscitation — reduces hyperchloraemic metabolic acidosis; contains potassium (important as diarrhoea causes hypokalaemia); lactate is metabolised to bicarbonate correcting acidosis; outcome benefits supported by WHO guidelines
medicines.add_potassium: Once urine output established: add 20-40 mEq/L KCl to IV fluids (diarrhoea causes significant potassium losses — hypokalaemia causes cardiac arrhythmia)

categories.purpose: WHO and UNICEF recommendation: all children under 5 years with acute diarrhoea should receive zinc supplementation for 10-14 days — the evidence is compelling and the intervention is safe, cheap, and widely available.
categories.evidence: Meta-analyses: zinc reduces diarrhoea duration by 25%, stool output by 30%, treatment failure by 42%; reduces risk of diarrhoeal recurrence for 2-3 months after treatment (rebuilds zinc body stores); mechanism: zinc is essential for mucosal healing, intestinal immune function, and tight junction protein expression maintaining gut barrier integrity

medicines.name: Zinc Sulphate / Zinc Acetate / Zinc Gluconate
medicines.dosage: Children under 6 months: 10 mg once daily × 10-14 days; Children 6 months to 5 years: 20 mg once daily × 10-14 days
medicines.use_case: ALL children under 5 years with acute diarrhoea in low-middle income countries (India) — regardless of cause (viral, bacterial, parasitic); zinc prevents malnutrition-related complications of diarrhoea; the WHO-UNICEF joint statement mandates zinc + ORS as the standard treatment for childhood diarrhoea globally
medicines.side_effects: Nausea and vomiting (give with food or ORS to reduce); metallic taste; dissolve tablet in small amount of ORS or breast milk for infants
medicines.india_note: Zinc dispersible tablets (20 mg) are included in India's Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness (IMNCI) programme; available free at government health centres; ASHA workers trained to distribute; price-affordable for supplementary private purchase

categories.category_name: Antiemetics — Control Vomiting to Enable ORS
categories.purpose: Reduce vomiting to enable oral rehydration therapy — the primary goal. Antiemetics facilitate ORS administration and reduce IV fluid requirements.

medicines.name: Ondansetron (5-HT3 Antagonist) — First-Line Antiemetic
medicines.form: Oral Dissolving Tablet (ODT — placed under tongue; ideal for vomiting children); Tablet; IV/IM injection
medicines.dosage: Children: Single oral dose — 0.15-0.2 mg/kg (max 8 mg); standard weight-based dosing: 8-15 kg: 2 mg; 15-30 kg: 4 mg; >30 kg: 8 mg; Adults: 4-8 mg orally or IV every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: Vomiting in gastroenteritis preventing ORS administration; the PIVOTAL TRIAL (Freedman et al., NEJM 2015): single dose oral ondansetron in children with vomiting and dehydration significantly reduced IV fluid requirement, hospitalisation, and return visits — now standard of care for paediatric gastroenteritis with vomiting
medicines.mechanism: 5-HT3 receptor antagonist — blocks serotonin-mediated vomiting reflex at chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) and peripheral gut vagal afferents
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: ondansetron reduces vomiting in gastroenteritis; facilitates ORS intake; reduces IV fluid need; reduces hospitalisation rate by 50% in children with vomiting gastroenteritis
medicines.side_effects: Headache; constipation (usually mild); QT prolongation (rare, clinical significance low at single standard doses)
medicines.note: ODT formulation (oral dissolving tablet) ideal — placed under tongue; dissolves without swallowing; works even with active vomiting

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.dosage: Children: 0.25 mg/kg up to 3 times daily; maximum 30 mg/day; maximum 1 week; Adults: 10 mg up to 3 times daily (not for children under 12 as first-line — use ondansetron)
medicines.use_case: Nausea and vomiting in gastroenteritis as adjunct; prokinetic; available widely in India; use short-term only

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10 mg orally or IV every 8 hours (adults); NOT recommended for children under 18 — high dystonia risk
medicines.use_case: Adults with vomiting in gastroenteritis; alternative to ondansetron; IV route useful in hospital settings
medicines.side_effects: Dystonia — particularly in young women and children; tardive dyskinesia with prolonged use; maximum 5 days

categories.category_name: Antibiotics — Targeted Therapy for Specific Infections
categories.purpose: Targeted antibiotic treatment for SPECIFIC bacterial gastroenteritis causes where evidence supports benefit — NOT empirical broad-spectrum treatment for all diarrhoea.
antibiotic_contraindications: Mild self-limiting bacterial gastroenteritis in immunocompetent adults
STEC/EHEC O157:H7 bloody diarrhoea (INCREASES HUS risk — absolute contraindication)
Non-typhoidal Salmonella mild illness in healthy young adults (prolongs faecal shedding)
Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (stop precipitating antibiotic; adding another antibiotic usually counterproductive)

medicines.name: Azithromycin — First-Line for Multiple Indications
medicines.dosage: Traveller's diarrhoea (adult): 1g SINGLE DOSE; Shigella (children): 20 mg/kg once daily × 3 days; Campylobacter: 500 mg once daily × 3-5 days; Cholera: 1g single dose (adult) or 20 mg/kg (child); Typhoid: 500 mg once daily × 7 days
medicines.use_case: PREFERRED first-line antibiotic for most bacterial gastroenteritis in India: (1) Most effective for traveller's diarrhoea (single dose); (2) First-line for Shigella in India (ICMR recommends azithromycin over fluoroquinolones for Shigella given very high fluoroquinolone resistance in India — 60-80% resistance); (3) First-line for Campylobacter (ciprofloxacin resistance >50% in many Indian centres); (4) Cholera; (5) Safe in children and pregnancy
medicines.mechanism: Macrolide antibiotic — inhibits 50S ribosomal subunit; bacteriostatic (bactericidal at high intracellular concentrations); excellent intracellular penetration; long tissue half-life enabling single or short-course treatment
medicines.resistance_advantage: Lower fluoroquinolone resistance compared to ciprofloxacin for Campylobacter and Shigella in India; azithromycin resistance is still relatively low (though emerging); preferred for empirical treatment in India

medicines.name: Ciprofloxacin — Alternative for Selected Indications
medicines.dosage: Salmonella bacteraemia: 500 mg twice daily × 7 days; Traveller's diarrhoea (non-SE Asia): 500 mg twice daily × 3 days; Cholera: 1g single dose
medicines.use_case: Salmonella (invasive/systemic); traveller's diarrhoea in settings where fluoroquinolone resistance is low (NOT recommended for Shigella or Campylobacter in India — high resistance); cholera (alternative)
medicines.resistance_warning: HIGH fluoroquinolone resistance in India: Shigella (60-80% resistant), Campylobacter (>50% resistant in many Indian centres) — DO NOT use ciprofloxacin empirically for these pathogens in India without sensitivity testing

medicines.name: Tetracycline / Doxycycline — Cholera Treatment
medicines.dosage: Tetracycline 500 mg four times daily × 3 days; Doxycycline 300 mg single dose (adults)
medicines.use_case: CHOLERA — first-line antibiotic for cholera in adults; reduces duration and shedding; reduces fluid requirements; doxycycline single dose preferred for adherence in field conditions
medicines.contraindications: Pregnancy; children <12 years (dental discolouration, bone effects)

medicines.name: Metronidazole — Giardia and Amoeba
medicines.dosage: Giardia: 400 mg three times daily × 5-7 days; Amoebic dysentery: 500-750 mg three times daily × 5-10 days (FOLLOWED BY diloxanide furoate 500 mg TDS × 10 days or paromomycin 500 mg TDS × 7 days — luminal agent to clear cysts); C. difficile (mild-moderate, second-line): 400 mg three times daily × 10 days
medicines.mechanism: Nitroimidazole — enters cells; forms reactive intermediates that damage DNA of anaerobic organisms and protozoa; bactericidal/protozoal
medicines.side_effects: Metallic taste (very common); nausea; DISULFIRAM-LIKE REACTION with alcohol (avoid ALL alcohol during treatment and 48 hours after); peripheral neuropathy (prolonged use)

medicines.name: Tinidazole — Giardia and Amoeba (Single-Dose Advantage)
medicines.dosage: Giardia: 2g SINGLE DOSE; Amoeba: 2g once daily × 2-3 days (followed by luminal agent)
medicines.use_case: Giardia (PREFERRED over metronidazole — single dose ensures adherence; superior tolerance; equivalent efficacy); Entamoeba histolytica; better tolerated than metronidazole
medicines.side_effects: Metallic taste; nausea; avoid alcohol 72 hours after tinidazole

medicines.name: Nitazoxanide
medicines.dosage: Adults: 500 mg twice daily × 3 days; Children 1-3 years: 100 mg twice daily × 3 days; Children 4-11 years: 200 mg twice daily × 3 days
medicines.use_case: Cryptosporidium (immunocompetent — first-line treatment; limited efficacy in severe immunocompromised); Giardia (alternative); broad antiprotozoal spectrum; also has antiviral activity against rotavirus and norovirus (modest evidence)
medicines.note: Urine and stools may turn yellow-green (harmless — nitazoxanide colour)

medicines.name: Oral Vancomycin — C. difficile Treatment (First-Line)
medicines.form: Oral capsule 125 mg; OR IV vancomycin reconstituted for oral use (oral route — NOT absorbed systemically — acts locally in colon)
medicines.dosage: Mild-moderate CDI: 125 mg orally four times daily × 10 days; Severe CDI: 500 mg orally four times daily × 10 days; Fulminant CDI (with ileus): oral vancomycin per NG tube + rectal vancomycin enema + IV metronidazole
medicines.use_case: FIRST-LINE treatment for C. difficile infection — all severity grades; superior to metronidazole (which is now second-line only); NOT absorbed from gut — acts directly in colon where C. difficile lives
medicines.note: IV vancomycin has NO effect on CDI — only ORAL/RECTAL route is effective; the drug must be delivered to the colon

medicines.name: Fidaxomicin (Oral) — C. difficile (Preferred for Recurrent CDI)
medicines.use_case: First or second episode CDI — PREFERRED over vancomycin when available because: 50% reduction in CDI recurrence rate compared to vancomycin (particularly important for the hypervirulent NAP1 strain); narrow spectrum (minimal disturbance to other gut flora); more expensive than vancomycin; recommended by IDSA/SHEA for first recurrence
medicines.note: Minimal systemic absorption; acts locally in colon; not available widely in India at present — vancomycin is standard first-line in India

medicines.name: Rifaximin — Traveller's Diarrhoea and IBS-D
medicines.dosage: Traveller's diarrhoea: 200 mg three times daily × 3 days; IBS with diarrhoea (IBS-D): 550 mg three times daily × 14 days
medicines.use_case: Non-invasive, non-febrile traveller's diarrhoea (ETEC) in adults — particularly in destinations where the pathogen is predominantly non-invasive; NOT appropriate for bloody diarrhoea, Campylobacter, or Salmonella; post-gastroenteritis IBS-D management
medicines.note: Non-absorbed antibiotic — acts locally in GI tract; minimal systemic side effects; minimal impact on systemic flora; excellent tolerability

categories.purpose: Reduce stool frequency and fluid losses for patient comfort — ONLY in appropriate indications; CONTRAINDICATED in multiple important situations.
categories.critical_contraindications: NEVER USE LOPERAMIDE in: BLOODY DIARRHOEA (dysentery — any cause); SUSPECTED STEC/EHEC O157:H7 (risk of HUS); HIGH FEVER >38.5°C WITH DIARRHOEA; CHILDREN UNDER 2 YEARS; C. DIFFICILE COLITIS; INVASIVE BACTERIAL COLITIS; SUSPECTED BOWEL OBSTRUCTION

medicines.name: Loperamide
medicines.dosage: Adults: 4 mg initial, then 2 mg after each loose stool; maximum 16 mg/day; Children >12 years: adult dose; NOT for children under 2; NOT for children 2-12 years without medical supervision
medicines.use_case: ONLY for: uncomplicated NON-BLOODY WATERY traveller's diarrhoea without fever; mild non-invasive watery diarrhoea in otherwise healthy adults; do NOT use more than 2 days without medical review
medicines.mechanism: Mu-opioid receptor agonist in gut; reduces intestinal motility and fluid secretion; does not cross blood-brain barrier at therapeutic doses
medicines.note: Diarrhoea serves as a protective mechanism to expel pathogens and toxins — premature cessation with loperamide when invasive bacteria are present retains bacteria and toxins, potentially causing toxic megacolon or HUS

medicines.name: Bismuth Subsalicylate
medicines.dosage: Adults: 30 mL or 2 tablets every 30-60 minutes; maximum 8 doses per day
medicines.use_case: Mild traveller's diarrhoea; reduces duration; mild antimicrobial properties against ETEC; prophylaxis for traveller's diarrhoea (reduces risk by 65%); antiemetic and antidiarrhoeal
medicines.side_effects: Black stools and black tongue (harmless — bismuth sulphide); tinnitus at excessive doses (salicylate)
medicines.contraindications: Children under 12 years (Reye's syndrome risk); aspirin allergy; pregnancy

categories.purpose: Restore gut microbiota disrupted by gastroenteritis or antibiotics; reduce diarrhoea duration; prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.

medicines.name: Saccharomyces boulardii
medicines.dosage: 250-500 mg twice daily × 7-14 days; administer concurrently with antibiotics (safe — it is a yeast, not susceptible to bacterial antibiotics)
medicines.use_case: Prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (reduces incidence by 50%); treatment of acute infectious diarrhoea (reduces duration by ~24 hours); C. difficile prevention and recurrence reduction (50% fewer CDI recurrences); well-studied
medicines.mechanism: Non-pathogenic yeast; secretes serine protease that degrades C. difficile toxin B receptor; stimulates IgA secretion; enhances brush border enzyme expression; immune modulation
medicines.evidence: Cochrane review: S. boulardii reduces acute diarrhoea duration by 31 hours in children; reduces C. difficile recurrence by 50%

medicines.name: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG)
medicines.use_case: Acute viral gastroenteritis in children (most evidence for rotavirus diarrhoea — reduces duration by 24 hours); antibiotic-associated diarrhoea prevention; traveller's diarrhoea prophylaxis
medicines.evidence: Multiple RCTs and Cochrane reviews: LGG reduces rotavirus diarrhoea duration significantly; widely recommended in paediatric gastroenteritis guidelines

medicines.name: Multi-Strain Probiotics
medicines.dosage: 1-2 capsules/sachets twice daily; during and 2 weeks after antibiotic course
medicines.use_case: Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea prevention; gut microbiome restoration after gastroenteritis and antibiotic use; general gut health support post-gastroenteritis

categories.category_name: Faecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) — Recurrent C. difficile
categories.purpose: Restoration of normal gut microbiota by transplanting stool from a healthy screened donor into the colon of a patient with recurrent CDI — the most effective treatment for recurrent C. difficile infection.
categories.description: FMT involves preparing a suspension of fresh or frozen stool from a carefully screened healthy donor and delivering it via colonoscope, enema, or oral capsule into the patient's colon. The healthy donor microbiota repopulates the colon, competitively excluding C. difficile and restoring normal colonisation resistance. Multiple RCTs show >90% resolution of recurrent CDI after FMT — dramatically superior to vancomycin (35-50%). FMT is recommended for all patients with 2 or more CDI recurrences.
categories.india_availability: FMT programmes are established at several major Indian hospitals (AIIMS Delhi, PGI Chandigarh, CMC Vellore, Asian Institute of Gastroenterology, Apollo); National Donor Programme protocols emerging; increasing availability
categories.evidence: Van Nood et al. (NEJM 2013): FMT achieved 94% resolution of recurrent CDI vs 31% vancomycin; multiple subsequent RCTs confirm >90% efficacy after 1 FMT for recurrent CDI

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Nutritional management in gastroenteritis has undergone a paradigm shift — the traditional 'rest the gut and starve' approach is now known to be harmful and counterproductive. Current evidence-based guidance emphasises: (1) EARLY REFEEDING within 4-6 hours of starting rehydration; (2) CONTINUING BREASTFEEDING in infants — never stop; (3) Age-appropriate normal food (not just broth); (4) AVOIDING prolonged dietary restriction which worsens malnutrition and slows mucosal recovery. The BRAT diet (Bananas, Rice, Applesauce, Toast) provides a useful framework but should not be the only food for more than 24-48 hours.
diet_and_nutrition.early_refeeding_evidence: WHO, ESPGHAN, AAP guidelines all recommend early refeeding: Early refeeding reduces illness duration; improves mucosal recovery (enterocytes need luminal nutrition for repair — particularly glutamine from dietary protein); reduces post-gastroenteritis malnutrition; does NOT worsen diarrhoea in most cases; particularly critical in malnourished children where continued dietary restriction is potentially life-threatening
diet_and_nutrition.breastfeeding_mandate: BREASTFEEDING MUST CONTINUE throughout gastroenteritis — never interrupt breastfeeding for diarrhoea; breastmilk provides: IgA (passive mucosal immunity against pathogens); lactoferrin (antimicrobial); lysozyme; oligosaccharides (prebiotic, anti-adhesive against pathogens); hydration; complete nutrition; the most protective dietary intervention available for infants with gastroenteritis

phase_1_acute_rehydration.timing: First 4-6 hours while ORS is being administered
phase_1_acute_rehydration.goal: Rehydrate — ORS is priority; small sips of ORS; ice chips if vomiting; once vomiting reduced — advance to soft foods
phase_1_acute_rehydration.allowed: ORS sachets; small sips of coconut water; ice chips; weak rice water (kanji); ginger tea (anti-nausea)

recommended_foods_recovery_phase.category: BRAT Diet Plus Indian Equivalents — Core Recovery Phase

items.food: Plain boiled white rice (or rice congee/kanji/khichdi)
items.benefit: Easily digestible; low fibre (does not stimulate gut motility further); absorbs excess fluid in stool; provides energy during illness; rice congee (kanji — very watery, overcooked rice) is gentler than solid rice and provides additional hydration; traditional Indian remedy with strong scientific rationale
items.frequency: Multiple small portions throughout the day; best tolerated as congee initially

items.food: Moong dal khichdi (rice + split mung bean)
items.benefit: Best early-recovery solid food for Indian patients — moong dal is the most easily digestible legume (lowest gas-producing oligosaccharide content among pulses); provides complete protein + carbohydrate; soft texture; anti-inflammatory; traditional Indian post-illness food with excellent scientific basis; small amount of ghee provides caloric density and fat-soluble vitamin absorption without overloading the gut
items.frequency: From first solid feeding — continue as main meal during recovery (days 1-5)

items.food: Banana (ripe — yellow/speckled)
items.benefit: Pectin (soluble fibre) helps firm stools and slow diarrhoea; potassium replacement (critical electrolyte lost in diarrhoea); fructooligosaccharides (prebiotic — supports gut flora recovery); easily digestible; provides energy; B vitamins; antacid properties; widely available and affordable
items.frequency: 1-2 ripe bananas per day during illness and recovery

items.food: Plain boiled or mashed potatoes (no butter, no spice)
items.benefit: Easily digestible starch; potassium; binding effect on stool; provides calories without gut irritation
items.frequency: From day 2-3 as appetite returns

items.food: Plain white toast or rusk (no butter initially)
items.benefit: Simple digestible carbohydrate; dry starch absorbs excess fluid; gentle on irritated gut
items.frequency: As tolerated when solid food is attempted

items.food: Stewed or baked apple / Applesauce (cooked)
items.benefit: Cooked apple provides pectin (anti-diarrhoeal soluble fibre); avoids raw apple which is higher in insoluble fibre; glucose for energy; Vitamin C; easily tolerated
items.frequency: As snack or dessert during recovery

items.food: Coconut water (tender coconut — nariyal pani)
items.benefit: Natural electrolyte drink; contains potassium (600 mg/cup), sodium, magnesium, glucose; near-isotonic; gentle on gut; well-tolerated during nausea; excellent natural supplement to ORS; widely available in India; superior to plain water for rehydration
items.frequency: 1-3 glasses per day during acute illness

items.food: Rice water (kanji) — water from boiling rice
items.benefit: Traditional Indian remedy with strong scientific rationale; provides glucose, starches, and some sodium; helps firm stools (rice starch absorbs water); WHO used rice-based ORS in cholera research (comparable efficacy to glucose-ORS for severe diarrhoea); electrolyte-containing fluid that reduces stool output; soothing for gut
items.preparation: Boil 1 cup rice in 6 cups water until rice is very soft; strain the water; can add small pinch of salt; drink warm throughout the day
items.frequency: As much as desired — the main oral fluid during acute illness in many Indian households

items.food: Ginger tea (Adrak chai)
items.benefit: Most evidence-based natural antiemetic (6-gingerol blocks 5-HT3 receptors — same mechanism as ondansetron); reduces nausea and vomiting; anti-inflammatory; mild antispasmodic; can 'abort' or reduce vomiting when taken at onset; warm fluid contributes to rehydration
items.preparation: 1-2 cm fresh ginger in 2 cups boiling water, steep 10 minutes, strain; small amount of honey; avoid milk initially
items.frequency: 2-4 cups daily during nausea phase

recommended_foods_recovery_phase.rationale: Gastroenteritis disrupts the normal protective gut microbiota; probiotic foods help restore Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium populations, reduce diarrhoea duration, and prevent antibiotic-associated dysbiosis

items.food: Plain fresh yogurt / Dahi (with live cultures)
items.benefit: Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. bulgaricus, Streptococcus thermophilus — probiotics that restore gut flora after gastroenteritis; reduce diarrhoea duration (Cochrane evidence); the bacterial lactase in yogurt makes it tolerable even in post-gastroenteritis lactose intolerance (unlike milk which worsens diarrhoea); provides protein for mucosal recovery
items.frequency: 1-2 small bowls from day 3 of illness; continue for 4-6 weeks during and after antibiotic course
items.note: START with plain yogurt (not sour curd) from day 3 of illness; EXCEPTION to dairy restriction — yogurt is ALWAYS safe during gastroenteritis

items.food: Buttermilk / Chaach (diluted yogurt)
items.benefit: Excellent Indian probiotic; well-tolerated even during active diarrhoea; probiotics; electrolytes; cooling; traditional post-diarrhoea remedy with strong scientific basis; easier to digest than solid yogurt; reduces diarrhoea duration
items.frequency: 1-2 glasses daily during recovery

items.food: Idli (plain — without sambar initially)
items.benefit: Fermented rice and lentil product with natural probiotics (Lactobacillus mesenteroides, Leuconostoc); soft, easily digestible texture; well-tolerated during recovery; gentle on inflamed intestinal mucosa; provides carbohydrate and plant protein
items.frequency: From day 3-4 of recovery; excellent solid food reintroduction

recommended_foods_recovery_phase.rationale: Nutritional rehabilitation is CRITICALLY important after gastroenteritis in children — particularly malnourished Indian children; malnutrition significantly worsens gastroenteritis severity and is worsened by gastroenteritis (the 'malnutrition-infection cycle')

items.food: Dal (moong, masoor), eggs, chicken (soft cooked)
items.benefit: High-quality complete protein for intestinal mucosal repair and immune function; zinc (reduces future diarrhoea episodes); glutamine (the primary fuel for intestinal enterocytes — stimulates mucosal repair); from day 3-5 of recovery
items.frequency: Daily protein inclusion from first full recovery day

items.food: Fortified cereal porridge (Sato Malt, Farex, Cerelac) for children
items.benefit: Iron-fortified; zinc-fortified; multiple micronutrients; easily digestible; calorie-dense; important for nutritional rehabilitation post-diarrhoea in children under 5; particularly important for malnourished children who cannot recover nutrition quickly from standard home diet alone
items.frequency: As per age-appropriate feeding guidelines; 2-3 times daily in recovery phase for young children

foods_to_avoid.reason: Gastroenteritis pathogens (particularly rotavirus, Giardia, Cryptosporidium) damage the brush border of small intestinal enterocytes → reduce lactase enzyme activity → SECONDARY LACTOSE INTOLERANCE; giving milk and dairy products during and after acute gastroenteritis causes osmotic diarrhoea worsening dehydration and prolonging illness; EXCEPTION: yogurt is ALWAYS safe because the bacteria in yogurt produce lactase themselves
foods_to_avoid.duration: Avoid milk, paneer, cheese, cream, and butter-rich food for 5-7 days; reintroduce gradually; yogurt from day 3; milk from day 7-10

foods_to_avoid.reason: Delay gastric emptying; worsen nausea; stimulate gut motility increasing diarrhoea; difficult to digest with impaired intestinal enzyme function
Capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors in inflamed intestinal mucosa → worsens pain and diarrhoea; prolongs inflammation
Insoluble fibre accelerates intestinal transit, worsening diarrhoea in acute phase; soluble fibre (from bananas, cooked apples) actually HELPS firm stools — the distinction is important
foods_to_avoid.examples: Raw vegetables; whole grain cereals; bran; raw salads; legumes in large quantities
foods_to_avoid.exception: Soluble fibre (banana, cooked apple, yogurt) is BENEFICIAL — do not restrict these

foods_to_avoid.food: Sugary Beverages and Fruit Juices (Full Strength)
foods_to_avoid.reason: High osmolarity from sugar causes osmotic diarrhoea; glucose excess draws water into the gut, worsening fluid losses; full-strength juice is particularly harmful in children — dilute 1:1 with water or avoid; sports drinks (Gatorade) are inappropriate for gastroenteritis rehydration (too much sugar, too little sodium)
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Use WHO ORS instead of sports drinks or fruit juices; coconut water is acceptable (naturally appropriate osmolarity)

foods_to_avoid.reason: Direct GI mucosal irritant; dehydrating (diuretic); impairs immune function; absolute contraindication during active gastroenteritis and with antibiotics (especially metronidazole — disulfiram reaction)
Caffeine stimulates GI motility (worsens diarrhoea); mildly diuretic; increases abdominal cramping; avoid strong chai and coffee during acute illness; weak dilute tea is usually tolerated

sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.day_0_to_1_acute_phase: ORS sachets as primary fluid (200-400 mL after every loose stool); coconut water; rice kanji (watery rice); ginger tea; ice chips if vomiting; NO solid food while actively vomiting and severely nauseous
sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.day_1_to_2_early_recovery: ORS continues; plain rice congee; ripe banana; plain white toast; kanji; coconut water; plain curd (probiotic from day 1-2 if tolerating solids); ginger tea
sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.day_2_to_3: Moong dal khichdi (soft); boiled potato; stewed apple; plain curd; banana; diluted coconut water; avoid milk, fried food, and spice
sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.day_3_to_5: Dal + plain rice; plain roti; boiled egg (scrambled); plain yogurt; soft idli; cooked vegetables (lauki, pumpkin — no heavy spice); plain chicken soup
sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.day_5_to_7: Normal soft diet reintroduction; avoid: raw salads, fried food, full-fat dairy, very spicy; include probiotics (yogurt, buttermilk) daily
sample_meal_plan_gastroenteritis.week_2_onwards: Normal balanced diet; avoid trigger foods; probiotics for 4-6 weeks; hydration maintained; zinc supplement (children under 5)

handwashing_the_single_most_effective_pr.overview: Handwashing with soap and water is the MOST EFFECTIVE single intervention to prevent gastroenteritis — reduces diarrhoeal disease transmission by 30-47% according to WHO estimates.
key_times: AFTER changing nappies or cleaning a child who has defaecated
AFTER coughing, sneezing, or blowing nose
AFTER handling raw meat, poultry, or eggs
AFTER touching animals or animal waste
handwashing_the_single_most_effective_pr.technique: Wet hands; apply soap; lather for minimum 20 seconds (scrub all surfaces including backs of hands, between fingers, under nails — hum 'happy birthday' twice); rinse thoroughly; dry with clean towel or air dry; use paper towel to turn off tap in public facilities
handwashing_the_single_most_effective_pr.soap_vs_sanitiser: SOAP AND WATER is superior to alcohol hand gel for: Norovirus (alcohol gel less effective — soap mechanically removes virus); C. difficile spores (alcohol does NOT kill spores — only soap and water removes them from hands); Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts (alcohol less effective). Use alcohol gel only when soap and water genuinely unavailable.
handwashing_the_single_most_effective_pr.india_context: Handwashing at critical times reduces childhood diarrhoea by 47% — the Swachh Bharat Mission and WASH programmes have significantly increased handwashing access in India; soap at handwashing facilities is a priority public health investment

water_and_food_safety: WATER: Drink only boiled, filtered, or bottled water when water quality is uncertain; boiling for 1 minute (3 minutes at altitude) kills all pathogens; ceramic or reverse osmosis filters effective; chlorination at 0.5 mg/L effective against most pathogens (NOT Cryptosporidium and Giardia — requires filtration or UV for these)

FOOD SAFETY: Cook food thoroughly (especially poultry, eggs, shellfish); avoid raw and undercooked meat; wash fruits and vegetables; maintain food at safe temperatures (below 5°C or above 60°C); separate raw and cooked food; proper refrigeration; do not leave cooked food at room temperature >2 hours
STREET FOOD: In India — choose stalls with high turnover (food freshly prepared); avoid pre-cooked food sitting at room temperature; 'eat it hot or don't eat it'
SHELLFISH: Raw shellfish (oysters, clams) are major HAV, norovirus, and Vibrio sources — cook thoroughly; avoid raw shellfish in endemic areas

isolation_and_exclusion.return_to_work_school: Stay home for 48 HOURS AFTER LAST EPISODE of diarrhoea or vomiting — this is the standard recommendation for all gastroenteritis
isolation_and_exclusion.food_handlers_healthcare_workers: Food handlers must stay off work for 48 hours after last symptoms AND may require negative stool cultures for specific pathogens (Salmonella typhi — typhoid carrier; Shigella in some settings) before returning

EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.norovirus: 48 hours after last symptoms — very contagious; strict hand hygiene on return
EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.salmonella_non_typhoidal: 48 hours after last symptoms; food handlers may need negative stool culture
EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.shigella: 48 hours after last symptoms; negative stool culture required for food handlers and healthcare workers
EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.c_difficile: While symptomatic; standard contact precautions in hospital; not necessarily excluded from community settings (spores shed asymptomatically — not practical to exclude long-term)
EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.typhoid: Until three negative consecutive stool cultures post-treatment (particularly for food handlers)
EXCLUSION_PERIODS_BY_PATHOGEN.hepatitis_a: 1 week after jaundice onset; exclude from food handling

swachh_bharat_sanitation_context.india_specific: India's Swachh Bharat Mission (Clean India Mission) 2014-2019 constructed 100+ million household toilets and dramatically reduced open defecation — the primary driver of faecal-oral gastroenteritis in rural India; areas that achieved open defecation free (ODF) status show significant reductions in childhood diarrhoea mortality; maintaining and using toilets is as important as their construction
swachh_bharat_sanitation_context.wash_interventions: Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) interventions combined reduce diarrhoeal disease by 50%; India's Jal Jeevan Mission aiming for tap water to every household by 2024 — piped treated water dramatically reduces waterborne gastroenteritis

managing_illness_at_home: PREPARE ORS CORRECTLY — always use 1 full litre of water per sachet; do not add extra ingredients; use within 24 hours
GIVE ORS AFTER EVERY LOOSE STOOL — do not wait for dehydration signs to appear; early ORS prevents dehydration

KEEP A REHYDRATION LOG for infants — record: number of loose stools; vomiting episodes; amount of ORS given; urine output (number of wet nappies); temperature — report to doctor if pattern is concerning
MAINTAIN ROOM TEMPERATURE — fever causes increased fluid losses; use paracetamol for fever reduction; avoid aspirin in children
CONTINUE BREASTFEEDING — the most important feeding instruction for infants; offer breast frequently

MONITOR FOR RED FLAG SIGNS — make a written list of warning signs (blood in stool; no urine >8 hours; confusion; very sunken eyes; very high fever; inability to keep any fluid down); go to hospital if any appear
HYGIENE WITHIN HOUSEHOLD — the infected person should use separate towel; frequent handwashing; clean bathroom with bleach solution; wash infected person's clothes/nappies separately in hot water

green_zone.criteria: Diarrhoea <5 stools/day; vomiting <3 episodes/day; able to tolerate ORS; no blood in stool; temperature <38.5°C; normal urine output; alert and active; no alarm features
green_zone.action: ORS after each loose stool; zinc for children; continue breastfeeding; bland diet; avoid dairy; monitor every 4-6 hours; reassess in 24-48 hours

yellow_zone.criteria: Diarrhoea >6-8 stools/day; persistent vomiting preventing ORS intake; signs of moderate dehydration (sunken eyes, dry mouth, decreased urine); fever 38.5-39.5°C; blood in stool first appearance; not improving at 48-72 hours; child under 2 years not improving at 24 hours
yellow_zone.action: GP or urgent care same day; supervised ORS; blood tests if needed; ondansetron for vomiting; stool culture if bloody diarrhoea or high fever; possible IV fluids

red_zone.status: EMERGENCY — Call 102/112 or Go to Emergency Department
criteria: Signs of severe dehydration: no urine >8 hours; very sunken eyes; unable to drink; confusion; rapid weak pulse; cold extremities; collapsed or unresponsive
Blood in stool in a child — especially if progressing to pallor and reduced urine output 5-7 days later (HUS)
Infant under 3 months with any gastroenteritis — immediate hospital assessment mandatory
Persistent vomiting for >24 hours with no fluid retained — severe dehydration risk
Confusion, altered consciousness in any age — dehydration shock
Cholera-like — massive voluminous rice-water diarrhoea (can lose litres per hour)

complications.description: The most common and most immediately lethal complication of gastroenteritis globally — responsible for the vast majority of the 1.5 million annual childhood deaths from diarrhoea. Rapid fluid and electrolyte losses lead to hypovolaemia, electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia causing cardiac arrhythmia; hyponatraemia causing cerebral oedema and seizures; hypoglycaemia causing brain injury in children), and cardiovascular collapse. Dehydration develops MUCH FASTER in infants and young children than adults — within hours.
complications.management: ORS (mainstay); IV Ringer's Lactate for severe dehydration; electrolyte correction; glucose for hypoglycaemia

complications.description: Life-threatening triad from Shiga toxin (STEC O157:H7 or Shigella dysenteriae type 1): (1) Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia; (2) Thrombocytopaenia; (3) Acute renal failure. Affects 5-15% of children with STEC O157:H7 infection. Presents 5-10 days AFTER bloody diarrhoea begins — as diarrhoea improves, the child becomes pale, stops urinating, develops bruising. 3-5% mortality; 25-30% develop long-term renal impairment.
complications.management: Supportive ONLY — no antibiotics; no antidiarrhoeals; IV fluids; red cell transfusion for severe anaemia; dialysis for severe AKI; eculizumab in severe cases; no role for plasma exchange in typical HUS (unlike atypical HUS)

complications.description: Functional bowel disorder developing in 5-25% of patients after acute gastroenteritis — characterised by altered bowel habits (IBS-D: diarrhoea predominant; IBS-C: constipation; IBS-M: mixed), abdominal pain, and bloating persisting >3 months after the acute infection has resolved. Campylobacter, Salmonella, and Giardia are the most important triggers of PI-IBS. Mechanisms include: persistent mucosal immune activation; altered gut microbiota; increased intestinal permeability; sensitised enteric nervous system.
complications.management: Low-FODMAP diet; antispasmodics; rifaximin (for diarrhoea-predominant PI-IBS); probiotics; psychological support (CBT); gut-directed hypnotherapy

complications.description: Sterile inflammatory arthritis developing 1-4 weeks after enteric infection — particularly from Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia (and genitourinary infections with Chlamydia trachomatis — Reiter's syndrome triad: arthritis + urethritis + conjunctivitis). Large joints of lower limbs predominantly; typically asymmetric oligoarthritis. Usually self-limiting (weeks to months); may become chronic in HLA-B27 positive individuals.
complications.management: NSAIDs (first-line); physiotherapy; DMARDs (sulfasalazine) for chronic reactive arthritis; antibiotics for the triggering infection do not reliably prevent reactive arthritis

complications.description: In developing countries — particularly India — malnutrition and gastroenteritis form a devastating bidirectional cycle: malnutrition impairs intestinal mucosal immunity → increases susceptibility to and severity of enteric infections → gastroenteritis causes further nutritional depletion (anorexia, malabsorption, increased metabolic demands) → worsened malnutrition → increased susceptibility. This cycle is the primary driver of childhood mortality from diarrhoea in India. Zinc, Vitamin A, and iron deficiencies are particularly important in impaired anti-enteric immunity.
complications.severity: Severe in malnourished children — significantly increases mortality
complications.management: Zinc supplementation (WHO mandatory recommendation — 20 mg/day × 10-14 days); Vitamin A supplementation in Vitamin A deficient children (reduces diarrhoea mortality by 20-30%); therapeutic feeding; intensive nutritional rehabilitation in severe acute malnutrition with diarrhoea (F-75 then F-100 therapeutic formulas)

complications.complication: Toxic Megacolon (C. difficile, Severe UC Flare)
complications.description: Life-threatening complication of fulminant C. difficile colitis (or severe ulcerative colitis exacerbated by infection) — transmural colonic inflammation with paralytic dilation of the colon (transverse diameter >6 cm on plain X-ray). Presents with: fever; tachycardia; abdominal distension; ABSENT BOWEL SOUNDS; reduced or no diarrhoea (paradoxically — colon no longer propelling contents); hypotension; sepsis. Risk of colonic perforation and fatal peritonitis.
complications.management: ICU; IV vancomycin + IV metronidazole; bowel rest; NG decompression; emergency colectomy if not improving within 48 hours or if perforation suspected

complications.description: Acute autoimmune ascending flaccid paralysis occurring 2-6 weeks after Campylobacter jejuni gastroenteritis. Campylobacter is the MOST COMMON identified trigger — 20-40% of GBS cases follow Campylobacter infection. Molecular mimicry: antibodies against Campylobacter lipo-oligosaccharides cross-react with gangliosides (GQ1b, GM1) in peripheral nerve myelin — demyelinating autoimmune attack. Can cause respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation (20% of severe GBS); 5% mortality; 20% residual weakness at 1 year.
complications.management: Recognise early — any ascending weakness, areflexia, or facial weakness 2-6 weeks after diarrhoea → urgent neurology referral; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) or plasmapheresis; ICU respiratory monitoring; rehabilitation

key_points: Children under 5 years are at highest risk of severe dehydration and death — they have higher proportional fluid requirements (100-120 mL/kg/day for infants vs 30-40 mL/kg/day adults); smaller fluid reserves; higher metabolic rate; less ability to increase fluid intake voluntarily
NEVER STOP BREASTFEEDING during gastroenteritis — continue on demand throughout illness; breastmilk provides immunity, hydration, and nutrition simultaneously
Ondansetron single oral dissolving dose has transformed paediatric gastroenteritis management — enables ORS administration by controlling vomiting; reduces hospitalisation by 50%
Zinc 20 mg/day × 10-14 days is MANDATORY for all children under 5 — WHO and UNICEF recommendation; widely available and free at government health centres in India

ROTAVIRUS VACCINE: most impactful preventive intervention for childhood gastroenteritis; 2-dose oral series (Rotarix/Rotavac) from 6 weeks; must complete by 8 months; available free at all government immunisation centres in India under UIP

POST-GASTROENTERITIS LACTOSE INTOLERANCE: very common in children (rotavirus, Giardia damage brush border reducing lactase); causes persistent diarrhoea after apparent recovery; avoid milk for 5-7 days; yogurt is safe (bacterial lactase); dilute formula if formula-fed (half-strength for 2-3 days — ALTERNATIVE: lactose-free formula if available)
Return to school/nursery: 48 hours after LAST episode of diarrhoea or vomiting
NEVER GIVE: loperamide to children under 2 years; aspirin; high-dose glucose drinks; plain water alone to severely dehydrated infants (worsens hyponatraemia)

Elderly patients are at high risk of severe dehydration from reduced thirst sensation; impaired renal concentrating ability; multiple comorbidities; polypharmacy (PPIs, diuretics — worsen dehydration risk)
C. DIFFICILE is predominantly a disease of the elderly on antibiotics — any antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in a patient over 65 should be tested for C. diff

Dehydration signs may be less obvious in the elderly — reduced skin turgor is normal in aged skin (less reliable sign); check blood pressure lying and standing (postural drop = dehydration); serum creatinine rising

NOROVIRUS in elderly care homes is extremely dangerous — outbreaks cause significant mortality; strict infection control (48-hour exclusion; bleach cleaning; isolation of symptomatic residents); cohorting in healthcare settings
Confusion and delirium from dehydration and electrolyte disturbances are common presenting features in elderly gastroenteritis — not just GI symptoms
Lower threshold for hospital admission; faster deterioration; multiple comorbidities

Listeria monocytogenes — most concerning bacterial pathogen in pregnancy; causes severe invasive gastroenteritis; miscarriage; premature birth; stillbirth; neonatal meningitis; any febrile illness after eating high-risk foods (soft cheese, deli meats, smoked fish) in pregnancy warrants URGENT assessment and empirical IV ampicillin
Salmonella and Campylobacter may cause bacteraemia in pregnancy — treat with azithromycin (safe in all trimesters); avoid fluoroquinolones
Dehydration in pregnancy triggers uterine contractions — severe gastroenteritis dehydration may precipitate preterm labour; aggressive IV fluid replacement essential

SAFE ANTIBIOTICS in pregnancy for gastroenteritis: amoxicillin; azithromycin; cefalexin; cephalosporins; ampicillin (Listeria); AVOID: fluoroquinolones (1st trimester — teratogenicity concerns); tetracycline; nitrofurantoin at term
ORS is safe in all trimesters; IV Ringer's Lactate for severe dehydration; paracetamol for fever
Norovirus and viral gastroenteritis — supportive management; monitor foetal heart rate in severe illness
Giardia in pregnancy: tinidazole preferred over metronidazole (metronidazole — avoid in 1st trimester if possible)

HIV/AIDS (CD4 <200): Cryptosporidium causes severe, chronic, life-threatening diarrhoea without effective specific antibiotic treatment; only effective treatment is immune reconstitution via ART; CMV colitis (bloody diarrhoea — diagnose by colonoscopy biopsy; treat with IV ganciclovir); atypical Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) — diarrhoea + fever + weight loss in AIDS; Microsporidia; Cyclospora
Organ transplant recipients: C. difficile is extremely common; CMV gastroenteritis; Cryptosporidium; lower threshold for investigations and treatment; risk of unusual organisms

Chemotherapy patients: C. difficile from prophylactic antibiotics and chemotherapy-related gut flora disruption; consider gut decontamination protocol changes; neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) — must be distinguished from infectious gastroenteritis
ALL immunocompromised patients with gastroenteritis require: hospitalisation; blood cultures; comprehensive stool PCR panel; endoscopy if not improving; early specialist involvement

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Rotavirus Vaccine — MOST IMPORTANT for Childhood Gastroenteritis
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose oral series (Rotarix or Rotavac): dose 1 at 6 weeks, dose 2 at 10-14 weeks; must complete by 8 months of age; NO catch-up after 8 months (safety concerns with vaccination at older age — intussusception risk)
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Rotavirus is the leading cause of severe childhood diarrhoea and dehydration globally — responsible for >78,000 child deaths annually in India alone (pre-vaccine era). Rotavirus vaccine is one of the most cost-effective public health interventions ever — reduces rotavirus hospitalisation by 85-95% in vaccinated cohorts; reduces all-cause childhood diarrhoea hospitalisations by 40-60%. Included in India's Universal Immunisation Programme (UIP) since 2016. Rotavac — India's own indigenously developed oral rotavirus vaccine (Bharat Biotech) — has equivalent efficacy to international brands at lower cost.
vaccinations_recommended.india_programme: Available FREE at all government immunisation centres across India; ASHA workers and ANMs administer at village health and nutrition days (VHND); coverage improving annually

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Typhoid Vaccine — Prevention of Enteric Fever
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Vi polysaccharide injectable: single dose; booster every 3 years; Typhoid Conjugate Vaccine (TCV — Typbar-TCV, Bharat Biotech): single dose from 6 months of age; provides longer protection; preferred for children
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Salmonella typhi (typhoid) is a major enteric pathogen in India — 4-6 million typhoid cases annually; causes severe prolonged febrile gastroenteritis leading to intestinal perforation and haemorrhage if untreated; typhoid fever is distinct from non-typhoidal Salmonella gastroenteritis but both are caused by Salmonella and relate to gut infection. TCV is safe from 6 months of age, provides better protection than old Vi polysaccharide vaccine, and requires only one dose — major improvement for childhood protection. India recently included TCV in UIP for children in some states.
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: All residents of typhoid-endemic areas (all of India); travellers to high-risk areas; food handlers; healthcare workers

vaccinations_recommended.vaccine: Hepatitis A Vaccine — Prevention of Viral Hepatitis with GI Onset
vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose series: dose 1 + booster at 6-18 months; lifelong protection
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis A virus (HAV) is transmitted via contaminated food and water (fecal-oral — same route as enteric gastroenteritis pathogens); presents with gastroenteritis-like prodrome (nausea, vomiting, anorexia, abdominal pain) followed by jaundice; highly prevalent in India; vaccine preventable. HAV vaccination is particularly important for: travellers; food handlers; people with chronic liver disease (HAV in cirrhosis is life-threatening); healthcare workers.
vaccinations_recommended.india_note: Not in India's UIP currently — available privately; cost approximately Rs 1,000-1,500 per dose; increasingly recommended in Indian paediatric and gastroenterology guidelines

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Shanchol (India-manufactured inactivated oral vaccine): 2 doses given 14 days apart; provides protection for 2-3 years; suitable for adults and children ≥1 year; Dukoral: 2 doses + 1 booster; provides some ETEC (traveller's diarrhoea) protection in addition to cholera
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Vibrio cholerae causes severe rapidly fatal watery diarrhoea in India — endemic in Bihar, West Bengal, Odisha; major outbreaks during flooding and monsoon; India is a cholera-endemic country. Shanchol — indigenously developed by SII (Serum Institute of India) — provides 65-80% protection for 2+ years; recommended by WHO for outbreak response and endemic area populations. India has deployed Shanchol during cholera outbreak response in Bihar and West Bengal.
vaccinations_recommended.recommended_for: Residents of cholera-endemic areas; pilgrimage participants (Kumbh Mela, Char Dham); humanitarian workers in flood-affected areas; travellers to endemic regions

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza causes significant GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain — 'gastric flu') in addition to respiratory symptoms; influenza can exacerbate gastroenteritis in co-infected patients; influenza vaccination reduces overall illness burden and may prevent secondary bacterial co-infections that worsen gastroenteritis; recommended for all healthcare workers who care for gastroenteritis patients
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Annual vaccination for healthcare workers; elderly; immunocompromised; pregnant women; children 6 months-5 years (highest gastroenteritis burden)

when_to_see_doctor: Any blood or mucus in stools — DO NOT manage at home without medical assessment; possible Shigella, Campylobacter, STEC, amoebic dysentery — some require specific antibiotics; others (STEC) should NOT receive antibiotics
Infant under 3 months with diarrhoea or vomiting — ALWAYS see a doctor SAME DAY; very limited fluid reserves; high risk of rapid deterioration
Child not able to keep any ORS down for more than 1-2 hours — vomiting everything; needs antiemetic (ondansetron) and/or IV fluids
Signs of moderate dehydration developing — sunken eyes, dry mouth, reduced urine output, increasingly lethargic — GP or urgent care same day
High fever >38.5°C with gastroenteritis — possible invasive bacterial infection requiring specific treatment
Diarrhoea lasting more than 3 days in children or 5-7 days in adults without improvement
Prolonged diarrhoea >14 days — possible parasitic infection (Giardia, Entamoeba, Cryptosporidium) — stool examination required
Recent use of antibiotics within 2 months AND new diarrhoea — possible C. difficile; stool toxin testing required
Immunocompromised patient (HIV, cancer, transplant) with any gastroenteritis — higher risk of severe and unusual infections
Recently returned from travel abroad with persistent diarrhoea >7 days — possible tropical infection (Giardia, Entamoeba, typhoid, Cyclospora)
Food handler or healthcare worker with gastroenteritis — occupational health requirements; potential source of outbreak; needs stool culture results before returning to work
Multiple people in the same household or institution ill simultaneously after eating the same food — suspected food poisoning outbreak; contact local health department or FSSAI food safety officer
emergency_signs: NO URINE OUTPUT for 8+ hours in a child, OR visibly very dark concentrated urine with sunken eyes and unable to drink — SEVERE DEHYDRATION — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112) IMMEDIATELY
INFANT UNCONSCIOUS, LIMP, OR UNABLE TO ROUSE — severe dehydration shock or electrolyte crisis — CALL 102/112
BLOOD IN STOOL IN A CHILD who was getting better but now becoming PALE, BRUISING, AND STOPPING URINATING 5-7 days after the onset — POSSIBLE HUS (Haemolytic Uraemic Syndrome) — PAEDIATRIC EMERGENCY
CONFUSION or ALTERED CONSCIOUSNESS in an adult or older child with gastroenteritis — dehydration shock; hyponatraemia; bacteraemia — EMERGENCY
RAPID WEAK PULSE, HYPOTENSION (feeling faint), COLD CLAMMY EXTREMITIES with gastroenteritis — DEHYDRATION SHOCK — CALL 102/112
MASSIVE PROFUSE WATERY DIARRHOEA — litres per hour — possible CHOLERA — EMERGENCY IV fluids; call 102/112
ASCENDING WEAKNESS or PARALYSIS in the legs, weeks after a diarrhoeal illness — possible GUILLAIN-BARRÉ SYNDROME post-Campylobacter — URGENT NEUROLOGY REFERRAL
SEVERE GENERALISED ABDOMINAL PAIN WITH RIGID ABDOMEN ('board-like') and absent bowel sounds in a patient with known C. difficile — POSSIBLE TOXIC MEGACOLON or PERFORATION — SURGICAL EMERGENCY
HIGH FEVER (>39°C) WITH RIGORS (violent shivering) AND BLOODY DIARRHOEA — POSSIBLE BACTERAEMIA — blood cultures and IV antibiotics needed URGENTLY
PREGNANT WOMAN with fever + gastroenteritis after eating soft cheese, deli meats, or smoked fish — POSSIBLE LISTERIA — OBSTETRIC AND INFECTIOUS DISEASE EMERGENCY

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between gastroenteritis and food poisoning?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Gastroenteritis is a broader term — inflammation of the stomach and intestines causing diarrhoea and vomiting from any cause, including viruses, bacteria, parasites, or their toxins. Food poisoning is specifically when illness is caused by eating contaminated food or drink. In practice there is significant overlap — most food poisoning IS a form of gastroenteritis. The key clinical distinction is timing: food poisoning from PRE-FORMED TOXINS (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) starts very quickly — within 1-6 hours of eating, with explosive vomiting as the dominant symptom. Gastroenteritis from viral infections (norovirus, rotavirus) or bacterial invasion has a longer incubation of 12 hours to several days. A useful rule: if multiple people who ate the same meal all become ill within 6 hours — think food poisoning from toxins; if illness develops 24-72 hours after eating and spreads through a household — think viral gastroenteritis or bacterial infection.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is ORS and why is it more important than any medicine?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) is a simple mixture of glucose, sodium, potassium, and water precisely formulated by the WHO. It exploits a biological mechanism that works even during severe diarrhoea — the sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT1) in the intestinal lining, which continues to absorb sodium coupled to glucose even when other absorption mechanisms are failing. This allows ORS to actually replace fluids and electrolytes that are being lost through diarrhoea and vomiting. ORS is quite literally the most life-saving medical invention for diarrhoeal disease — it has prevented an estimated 1 million childhood deaths per year since its introduction. It is more important than any antibiotic, antidiarrhoeal, or other medication for most cases of gastroenteritis. In India, ORS sachets (branded as Electral, Nimwali, or generic ORS) are available at all chemists for a few rupees. The critical rules: always dissolve one sachet in EXACTLY 1 full litre of clean water; never add extra sugar or salt; give after every loose stool and vomiting episode.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I give antibiotics for diarrhoea and when should I NOT?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Antibiotics are appropriate only in specific situations: (1) BLOODY DIARRHOEA (dysentery) — likely Shigella, Campylobacter, or amoeba — azithromycin for Shigella and Campylobacter in India; metronidazole/tinidazole for amoeba; (2) CHOLERA — all cases (azithromycin or doxycycline); (3) TYPHOID FEVER — azithromycin or ceftriaxone; (4) C. DIFFICILE — oral vancomycin; (5) TRAVELLER'S DIARRHOEA that is severe. When antibiotics are NOT appropriate and should NOT be given: (1) Viral gastroenteritis (90% of cases — antibiotics have zero effect against viruses); (2) Mild self-limiting watery diarrhoea in healthy adults; (3) STEC/bloody diarrhoea from E. coli O157:H7 — antibiotics dramatically increase the risk of HUS (kidney failure) — this is an absolute contraindication. In India, a very important point: Shigella and Campylobacter are now highly resistant to ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones) in many areas — azithromycin is the preferred antibiotic for these organisms, not ciprofloxacin.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My 2-year-old has diarrhoea and vomiting — what should I do at home and when should I go to hospital?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most important thing is giving ORS (Oral Rehydration Solution) immediately — not plain water, not cola drinks, not sports drinks. ORS sachets from the chemist: dissolve 1 sachet in exactly 1 litre of boiled and cooled water. If your child is vomiting — give ORS very slowly, 5-10 mL (1-2 teaspoons) every 2-5 minutes by spoon or syringe. Even if they vomit, most of that small amount was absorbed. Continue breastfeeding if you are breastfeeding. Give 1 teaspoon of zinc (20 mg) daily for 10-14 days (government health centres provide this free). Avoid giving milk, formula, or solid food until vomiting has improved. WHEN TO GO TO HOSPITAL IMMEDIATELY: your child has no wet nappy for 6+ hours; eyes are very sunken; mouth is bone dry with no saliva; child is not responding normally or very difficult to rouse; fever above 39°C; blood in the stool; refuses to take any ORS at all; vomiting is so severe that nothing stays down for more than 1-2 hours. Infants under 3 months with any vomiting or diarrhoea should be seen by a doctor the same day.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is C. difficile and why is it becoming a problem?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) is a bacterium that lives in the gut of some people without causing problems — but when antibiotics disrupt the normal protective gut bacteria, C. diff can overgrow and produce toxins that cause severe diarrhoea and colitis. The symptoms are frequent watery diarrhoea (3+ times daily), abdominal cramping, and sometimes fever, developing during or within 8 weeks of antibiotic use. C. diff is increasingly recognised in India as antibiotic use has increased dramatically. It is particularly dangerous in elderly patients in hospitals. Important facts: It forms spores that survive on surfaces for months — killed by bleach but NOT by alcohol hand sanitiser; handwashing with soap and water is essential for C. diff prevention. It should be treated with oral vancomycin (not IV vancomycin which doesn't reach the colon). The most effective treatment for repeat C. diff infections is Faecal Microbiota Transplantation (FMT) — now available at several major Indian hospitals — which cures >90% of recurrent cases.

frequently_asked_questions.question: How can I prevent gastroenteritis during travel in India?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The five golden rules for safe travel in India: (1) DRINK SAFE WATER — bottled water (check seal is intact) or boiled water for drinking, brushing teeth, making ice; avoid tap water, well water, or drinks with ice of unknown source; (2) COOK IT or PEEL IT — eat food that is freshly cooked and served hot; peel fruits yourself; avoid pre-peeled, pre-cut, or pre-packaged fresh fruits from uncertain sources; (3) CHOOSE BUSY STREET FOOD STALLS with high turnover and food cooked fresh in front of you — high turnover means food is not sitting out; (4) WASH HANDS thoroughly with soap and water before eating and after using the toilet — always carry a small bar of soap; (5) AVOID RAW: raw salads, raw vegetables, raw shellfish, raw meat, unpasteurised dairy. Carry an ORS sachet, a zinc tablet (for children), and azithromycin for emergencies. The rotavirus, typhoid, and hepatitis A vaccines provide important additional protection — ensure your vaccinations are up to date before travel.
